en: The Lamp of the Doctrine of the Lord of Ascetics.
Now, the first chapter:
The Invocation of Auspiciousness.
I praise Śrī Veṅkaṭeśa, the Lord of Karīśaila; Śrī Devarāja, the Lion of Ghaṭikādri;
and the King of Sages (Rāmānuja) together with Kṛṣṇa—those supreme teachers of mine whom I beheld in a dream. ||1||
Having prostrated before the Lord of Ascetics, the great preceptor Vedāntārya, I compose this *Yatīndramatadīpikā* for the sake of the instruction of the simple-minded. (2)

This *Śārīrakaparibhāṣā*, titled *Yatīndramatadīpikā* (The Lamp of the Doctrine of the Lord of Ascetics), follows the Vedānta and is intended for the instruction of beginners, in accordance with the views of Vyāsa, Bodhāyana, Guhadeva, Bhāruci, Brahmanandin, Dramiḍācārya, Śrī Parāṅkuśanātha, Yāmunamuni, Yatīśvara, and others, who established through Vedic statements the following: that the non-dual reality (*advaita-tattva*) is the glorious Nārāyaṇa Himself as qualified by the sentient and the insentient; that He alone, when pleased by devotion (*bhakti*) and surrender (*prapatti*), is the means (*upāya*); and that He alone, as qualified by the non-material realm, is the goal to be attained (*prāpya*).
I, relying on the compassion of the Great Teacher, shall briefly elucidate this *Padārthasamuddeśa* according to my understanding.

All categories of reality (*padārtha*) are divided into two types by way of the distinction between the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of knowledge (*prameya*). The means of knowledge are exactly three. The object of knowledge is twofold, due to the distinction between substance (*dravya*) and non-substance (*adravya*). Substance is twofold: insentient (*jaḍa*) and sentient (*ajaḍa*). The insentient is twofold: primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and time (*kāla*). Primordial nature consists of twenty-four principles (*tattva*). Time, however, is threefold according to the distinction of its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). The sentient, moreover, is twofold: the transcendent (*parāk*) and the immanent (*pratyak*).

The Supreme (parāg) is also twofold: eternal manifestation (nityabhūti) and knowledge as an attribute of Dharma (dharmabhūtajñāna). The Inner Self (pratyag) is also twofold, due to the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara). The individual soul is threefold, due to the distinction between the bound (baddha), the liberated (mukta), and the eternally free (nitya). The bound is also twofold, due to the distinction between those seeking worldly enjoyment (bubhukṣu) and those seeking liberation (mumukṣu). Those seeking worldly enjoyment are twofold: those intent on wealth and desire (arthakāma) and those intent on religious duty (dharma). Those intent on religious duty are twofold: those intent on other deities and those intent on the Blessed Lord (bhagavat). Those seeking liberation are twofold: those intent on isolation (kaivalya) and those intent on final release (mokṣa).

One intent on liberation (*mokṣapara*) is of two kinds: the devotee (*bhakta*) and the one who has surrendered (*prapanna*). The one who has surrendered is of two kinds: the single-minded (*ekāntin*) and the supreme single-minded (*paramaikāntin*). The supreme single-minded is of two kinds, distinguished as the haughty (*dṛpta*) and the afflicted (*ārta*). The Lord (*īśvara*) is fivefold, according to the distinction of the Supreme (*para*), the Manifestation (*vyūha*), the Splendor (*vibhava*), the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*), and the Incarnation (*arcāvatāra*). The Supreme is of one kind. The Manifestation is fourfold, according to the distinction of Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha. Other manifestations such as Keśava and so forth are included within this very [fourfold] manifestation. The incarnations such as the Fish (*matsya*) and others are, moreover, infinite. The Inner Controller resides within every body.

The *arcāvatāra* (incarnation in the form of an image), however, refers to specific forms that have become objects of the eyes of all humanity, such as those at Śrīraṅga, Veṅkaṭādri, Hastigiri, Yādavādri, Ghaṭikācala, and so forth. *Adravya* (non-substance), on the other hand, is of exactly ten kinds, distinguished by the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, as well as touchlessness, color, taste, smell, conjunction, and power. Thus, after the enumeration of the categories, the definitions and examinations are now undertaken;
for those categories thus enumerated, the definition and examination are performed according to the order of their enumeration.

Regarding the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): the instrument of valid cognition is the *pramāṇa*. The *pramāṇa* is the definiendum (*lakṣya*). Being the instrument of valid cognition is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*). [Next,] the definition of valid cognition (*pramā*).

Valid cognition (*pramā*) is knowledge that conforms to conventional usage as it truly exists. Valid cognition is the definiendum (*lakṣya*); being knowledge that conforms to conventional usage as it truly exists is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*). If one were to say simply that "knowledge is valid cognition," there would be the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the cognition "this is silver" with respect to mother-of-pearl. Therefore, it is said "conforming to conventional usage. Even so, there would still be over-extension to that very same case, because during a state of delusion, the conventional usage "this is silver" is indeed employed. Therefore, it is said "as it truly exists."

By the phrase "as it actually exists" (*yathāvasthita*), doubt, erroneous cognition (*anyathājñāna*), and contrary cognition (*viparītajñāna*) are excluded. Regarding the qualified subject (*viśiṣṭe dharmiṇi*), there is the cognition: "Is this a post or a person? Erroneous cognition (*anyathājñāna*) is the inversion of the property (*dharma-viparyāsa*). For example: establishing through fallacious arguments that agency—which appears as a property of the self—is illusory. Contrary cognition (*viparītajñāna*) is the inversion of the substratum (*dharmin-viparyāsa*). For example: cognizing one thing as another thing. These are the three defects of a definition (*lakṣaṇa*).

A definition has three defects: under-extension (*avyāpti*), over-extension (*ativyāpti*), and impossibility (*asambhava*). Under-extension is the non-application of a definition to a portion of the object to be defined. Over-extension is its application to things other than the object to be defined. Impossibility is its non-application to the object to be defined anywhere at all. For example, if it is said that "the individual soul (*jīva*) is subject to the three qualities (*guṇa*)," there is under-extension. If it is said that "it possesses the quality of knowledge," there is over-extension. If it is said that "the individual soul is an object of the eye," there is indeed impossibility. Because these three stated defects are absent, the definition of valid cognition (*pramā*) is well-established. [Now follows] the analysis of the category of instrument (*karaṇa*).

The most effective means is the instrument (*karaṇa*). That which is an exceptionally effective means is the "most effective" (*sādhakatama*). That in the presence of which knowledge arises without delay is said to be "exceptional. By this, it is established that the instrument of valid cognition (*pramā*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

As for the refutation of the definition of valid cognition composed by Dharmarājādhvarīndra—such as the claim that "the means of valid cognition is that which apprehends an object not previously cognized"—it is to be disregarded because it has already been rejected by the respective proponents of those views themselves.
Regarding the number of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) accepted by Viśiṣṭādvaita:
those means of valid cognition are only three, namely perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and verbal testimony (*śabda*).
[Now follows] the definition of the means of valid cognition that is perception.

In this context, perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*) for direct valid cognition (*sākṣātkāri-pramā*). The term "direct" (*sākṣātkārī*) is used to exclude inference (*anumāna*) and other means of knowledge; the term "valid" (*pramā*) is used to exclude cognitions produced by the senses when they have already perceived their object (i.e., non-valid memory). Thus, perception is defined by its two divisions: indeterminate (*nirvikalpaka*) and determinate (*savikalpaka*).

And that perception is of two kinds, distinguished as non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) and conceptual (*savikalpaka*). Non-conceptual perception is the initial apprehension of an individual object (*piṇḍa*) as qualified by qualities, configuration, and so forth. Conceptual perception, however, is the apprehension of a second and subsequent individual objects as qualified by qualities, configuration, and so forth, accompanied by reflective recognition (*pratyavamarśa*). Both of these have only qualified objects as their domain, because a cognition that grasps an unqualified [object] is neither observed nor logically possible. This is the manner in which things are apprehended.

The process of apprehension is as follows: the self (ātman) comes into contact with the mind (manas), the mind with the sense organ (indriya), and the sense organ with the object (artha). This is because it is a rule that the sense organs function by reaching their objects. Therefore, when there is contact between an object such as a jar and a sense organ such as the eye, visual cognition arises in the form "this is a jar" or "this is a cloth. The same applies to tactile perception and other types of direct perception. Regarding the analysis of the relationship: in the apprehension of a substance (dravya), the relationship is conjunction (saṃyoga). Since inherence (samavāya) is not accepted [as the cause] for the apprehension of qualities like color residing in a substance, the relationship in that case is based on being supported by what is conjoined (saṃyuktāśrayaṇa).
The sub-divisions of perception:

Perception is twofold, distinguished as non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) and conceptual (*savikalpaka*), and further divided into that which is mundane (*arvācīna*) and that which is super-mundane (*anarvācīna*). The mundane, moreover, is twofold: dependent on the sense organs and independent of them. That which is independent of the senses is twofold: self-established (*svayaṃsiddha*) and divine (*divya*). The self-established is produced by yoga; the divine is produced by the grace of the Lord. The super-mundane, however, is the eternal knowledge of the liberated souls (*muktātman*) and the ever-liberated (*nityamukta*). The super-mundane has been mentioned here incidentally.
Thus, it is established that perception is the instrument for producing direct valid cognition (*sākṣātkāri-pramā*).
Memory is included within perception.

If it is objected: "It has been stated that valid knowledge (*pramā*) is cognition that accords with the actual state of affairs as they are conventionally established. Since memory (*smṛti*) is also a cognition that accords with the actual state of affairs as they are conventionally established, and since memory is also enumerated among the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), how can it be maintained that there are only three means of valid knowledge? The answer is: Even if the validity of memory is admitted, because it depends upon a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) and is rooted in perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is subsumed under its source, namely perception. Therefore, it is not postulated as a separate means of valid knowledge. Thus, it is possible that there are only three means of valid knowledge. This concludes the definition of memory.

Memory (*smṛti*) is defined as a cognition produced solely by a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) generated by a prior experience. In this regard, the cause is the awakened latent impression. And the awakening of the latent impression is brought about by such factors as the perception of a similar object, unseen destiny (*adṛṣṭa*), or reflection; as it has been stated, memory occurs in some cases from the sight of a similar thing, in some from unseen destiny, and in some from reflection. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), association (*sāhacarya*) is also included, and thus memory may also arise from that.

The first [type of memory] arises from similarity, as for example, the recollection of Yajñadatta upon seeing Devadatta, when the two are similar. The second is, for example, the recollection of a divine place such as Śrīraṅga, which was experienced at some other time or in another location by chance. The third is, for example, the recollection of the beautiful and auspicious divine form of Śrī Veṅkaṭeśa while He is being meditated upon. The fourth, however, is the recollection of one of two people who are associated together, such as Devadatta and Yajñadatta, upon seeing the other.

There is a rule that everything correctly experienced necessarily becomes an object of memory. In some cases, however, due to the lapse of time or the obscuration of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) by illness and so forth, there is an absence of memory.
This is the manner in which perception, recognition, and other such cognitions are included within the category of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Just as memory is included within perception (*pratyakṣa*), so too is recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)—such as "this is that same Devadatta"—included within perception. In our view, since non-existence (*abhāva*) is of the nature of another positive entity (*bhāvāntara*), the cognition of it is also included within perception. The absolute non-existence of a jar on the ground is the ground itself; the prior non-existence of a jar is simply the clay; and the destruction of a jar is simply the potsherd. The inference (*ūha*) is generally expressed as: "This person must be [the one] by this name."

The indeterminate cognition, "What is the name of this tree standing before me?", is called doubt (*saṃśaya*). Both of these [indeterminate and doubtful cognitions] are included within perception (*pratyakṣa*). Intuition (*pratibhā*) residing in a meritorious person is also included within perception.
This is the establishment of the theory of true manifestation (*yathārthakhyāti*).

Since it has been stated that "all cognition is in accordance with reality (*yathārtha*)—this is the view of those who know the Vedas"—cognitions such as perceptual error and the like are indeed *yathārtha*. This is because [the author] refutes the proponents of non-apprehension (*akhyāti*), self-apprehension (*ātmakhyāti*), the theory of the indeterminable (*anirvacanīyakhyāti*), misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*), and the apprehension of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*), and instead accepts the position of the apprehension of the existent (*satkhyāti*). The apprehension of the existent means that the object of cognition is real. If one asks, "In that case, how can there be erroneousness? [the answer is: erroneousness arises from the sublation of the practical usage regarding the object. We shall demonstrate this.

Because all elements exist everywhere within earth and the other elements through the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*), the object of knowledge is real. In that regard, the cessation of error occurs through the cognition of the predominance of the silver-portion. Furthermore, dream-cognition and the like are indeed real; for it is understood from scripture that the Supreme Person creates chariots and so forth—limited by specific times and experienced by particular individuals.

In cases such as "the conch is yellow," the ocular rays, mixed with the bile-substance residing in the eye, come into contact with the conch and other objects. Therein, the whiteness residing in the conch is not perceived because it is overwhelmed by the yellowness residing in the bile. Consequently, the conch is cognized as "yellow," like a conch smeared with gold.

Because of its subtlety, the yellowness is perceived by one's own eyes alone as it issues forth from them, and not by others. Even a crystal gem situated near a *japā* flower is perceived as red; that cognition is indeed real. Likewise, the cognition of water in a mirage is also explained through the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*), as previously stated. The process of quintuplication will be explained later. The same applies to the illusion regarding the directions.

This is because one direction exists within another direction, and because no distinct substance called "direction" is admitted apart from its delimiting factors. As for the case of a fire-brand wheel (*alātacakra*) and the like, it is due to extreme rapidity that the intervening spaces are not perceived; thus, the various objects themselves, as they come into contact with those respective locations, are apprehended in the form of a circle. That too is indeed real. Even the perception of one's own face and so forth in mirrors and the like is accurate. The visual rays, their course being reflected by the mirror and such, first apprehend the mirror and then apprehend one's own face and so forth.

Even in that case, such a perception occurs because the intermediate space is not apprehended due to extreme rapidity. In the cognition of two moons and similar instances as well, there are two distinct causal complexes (*sāmagrī*)—each independent of the other—that serve as the cause for the perception of two moons, arising from a difference in the movement of the visual light caused by factors such as pressing on the eye with a finger or ophthalmia (*timira*). This dual causal complex is ultimately real (*pāramārthika*), and it is by means of this that the cognition of two moons arises. Therefore, all cognition is true and has a qualified object (*saviśeṣa-viṣaya*), because an object devoid of qualifications (*nirviśeṣa-vastu*) is never apprehended;
even by the first moment of perception, it is only an object qualified by difference that is grasped.

Such direct perception first grasps [the object] as qualified by distinctions such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth. In the conventional usage of the term "distinction," however, there is a dependence upon a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), but not in its essential nature (*svarūpeṇa*). Therefore, neither the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) nor the fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) exists. Infinite regress consists in a succession of dependencies;
mutual dependence refers to the case where, for example, the cognition produced by the sentence "You are the tenth" is denied the status of being a direct perception because it depends on another.

Objection: Why should this statement, "You are the tenth," not also be a case of perception? Reply: No; for although the word "you" (*tvam*) refers to something perceived, the phrase "are the tenth" (*daśamo'si*) is produced by verbal testimony (*vākya*). If the phrase "are the tenth" were to have perception as its object—that is, if it were itself a perception—then the statement "You possess dharma" (*dharmavāṃstvamasīti*) would also have to be a perception. This would lead to an undesirable over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) even if such a claim were accepted. For this very reason, the sentence "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) does not produce immediate, non-conceptual knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*). This concludes the refutation of the views of both the Advaitins and the Naiyāyikas regarding objects of perception.

By this, the following false doctrinal constructions are refuted: "The instrument of valid perceptual cognition is perception; and here, valid cognition (*pramā*) is consciousness itself (*caitanya*). Consciousness is threefold: consciousness delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), consciousness delimited by the mental modification (*vṛtti*), and consciousness delimited by the object. When there is identity among these three, then direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*) occurs. Furthermore, that [intuition] has only the featureless (*nirviśeṣa*) as its object and grasps only non-difference (*abheda*)," and so forth.

The view of the Naiyāyikas—that indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*) is a cognition devoid of association with name, genus, and so forth, which apprehends the mere thing as "this is something"—is also refuted. This constitutes the Naiyāyika position of exclusion.

If it is objected: "Since it has been said that 'the systems of Kaṇāda and Pāṇini are beneficial to all treatises,' how can there be a refutation of the doctrine of Gautama? We reply: Indeed, we do not effect a total refutation of this system. Whatever herein is consistent with reason is accepted, just as one makes use of the water in a tank while constructed by another, yet certainly does not accept even the mud within that tank.

Beyond this, we do not accept such doctrines that contradict the Sūtrakāra and others—such as the theory of atoms as the ultimate cause, the view that the Vedas have a personal author, the view that Īśvara is known through inference, the view that the soul is all-pervasive, the acceptance of generality (*sāmānya*), particularity (*viśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*) as distinct categories (*padārtha*), the postulation of comparison (*upamāna*) and so forth as independent means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the postulation of number, dimension, separateness, disjunction, priority, posteriority, gravity, fluidity, and so on as distinct qualities (*guṇa*), and the postulation of space (*diś*) as a substance (*dravya*). However, we do accept those [doctrines] that are not contradictory; thus, there is no inconsistency.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Definition of Perception," within the *Yatīndramatadīpikā*, composed by Śrīnivāsadāsa, the foremost disciple of the illustrious Mahācārya, the ornament of the Vādhūla lineage, concerning the technical terminology of the *Śārīraka* [Brahma-sūtras].
Now begins the second section:
the definition of inference (*anumāna*) and the definition of inferential cognition (*anumiti*).

Now, inference is being defined. Inferential cognition is the valid knowledge of a specific pervader (*vyāpaka*) resulting from the consideration of the state of being pervaded (*vyāpyatva*). The instrument for that [cognition] is inference. From the consideration of the state of being pervaded—of smoke, which is pervaded by fire—there arises the valid knowledge of the specific pervader, namely, the valid knowledge of fire.

The definition of pervasion (*vyāpti*): that which is restricted to no more extensive space and time is the *vyāpya* (the pervaded); that which exists in no less extensive space and time is the *vyāpaka* (the pervader). Thus, this *vyāpya* is that which is invariably concomitant (*avinābhūta*), and the *vyāpaka* is its counter-correlative. By this, it is stated that pervasion is a relation determined by the absence of any limiting condition (*upādhi*). This very pervasion—namely, "wherever there is smoke, there is fire"—is apprehended through repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*). Pervasion is twofold, distinguished as positive (*anvaya*) and negative (*vyatireka*).

Pervasion (*vyāpti*) that functions in the form of a positive concomitance between the means of proof (*sādhana*) and the thing to be proven (*sādhya*) is positive pervasion (*anvayavyāpti*). For example: "Whatever possesses smoke possesses fire. Pervasion that functions in the form of a negation of the means of proof upon the negation of the thing to be proven is negative pervasion (*vyatirekavyāpti*). For example: "Whatever is without fire is without smoke. Both types of this pervasion are defective when a limiting condition (*upādhi*) is possible. [The following is] the definition of a limiting condition (*upādhi*).

An *upādhi* (limiting condition) is that which, while pervading the probandum (*sādhya*), does not pervade the probans (*sādhana*). For example, when smoke is being proved by fire, "contact with wet fuel" is an *upādhi*. When dark complexion is being proved by being the son of Maitra, "being produced by the cooking of vegetables" is an *upādhi*. Furthermore, that *upādhi* is of two kinds: certain (*niścita*) and suspected (*śaṅkita*). An example of a certain one is as follows: "The service under dispute is a cause of suffering, because it is service, like service to a king"—here, "being undertaken out of sin" is the *upādhi*.

Since this [condition] is not present in the case of service to the Lord (*īśvara-sevā*), it is a "certain condition" (*niścita-upādhi*). An example of a "suspected condition" (*śaṅkita-upādhi*) is as follows: "The soul in question will attain liberation at the end of this body, because he has perfected his meditative absorption (*samādhi*), like Śuka and others. Here, the complete exhaustion of karma is the condition. Since it is doubtful whether that complete exhaustion of karma exists or does not exist in the soul in question who has perfected his meditative absorption, it is called a "suspected condition" due to its state of uncertainty. Therefore, it is established that the pervaded (*vyāpya*) is that which possesses a relationship free from such conditions. This concludes the definition of the pervaded.

The pervaded (*vyāpya*), the means of proof (*sādhana*), and the mark (*liṅga*) are synonymous. It has two forms which constitute the limbs of inference: pervasion (*vyāpti*) and subsistence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*). There are also five forms, which are: subsistence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), existence in the similar instance (*sapakṣe sattvam*), exclusion from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣād vyāvṛttiḥ*), having an uncontradicted object (*abādhitaviṣayatvam*), and having no counter-balancing argument (*asatpratipakṣatvam*). The subject (*pakṣa*) is the locus qualified by the property sought to be proved. For example, in the proof of [the mountain's] possession of fire and so forth, it is the mountain and the like.

The *sapakṣa* (similar instance) is that which possesses a property similar to the property sought to be proven (*siṣādhayiṣitadharma*). For example: the kitchen and so forth. The *vipakṣa* (dissimilar instance) is that which is devoid of the property to be proven and its kind. For example: a great lake and so forth. "Contradiction of the subject" (*bādhitaviṣayatva*) consists in the established absence of the property to be proven in the subject (*pakṣa*) by means of a powerful means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For example: "A great lake possesses fire," and so forth. "Non-contradiction of the subject" (*abādhitaviṣayatva*) consists in the presence of the absence of that [property to be proven] in the subject. "Lack of a counter-balanced opponent" (*asatpratipakṣatva*) consists in the absence of opposition from a means of valid cognition that appears to be of equal strength. These are the distinctions regarding the pervasion (*vyāpti*).

The pervaded (*vyāpya*) of such a nature is of two kinds, distinguished as *anvayavyatirekin* (positive-negative) and *kevalānvayin* (purely positive). That which possesses the five previously mentioned characteristics is the *anvayavyatirekin*. For example: "The mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke; whatever possesses smoke possesses fire, as in the case of a kitchen; whatever lacks fire lacks smoke, as in the case of a lake. That very same kind of pervaded which is devoid of a counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is the *kevalānvayin*. For example: "The object denoted by the word 'Brahman' exists because it is a real entity (*vastu*), like a jar."

Because there is no counter-example (vipakṣa), the purely positive (kevalānvayi) inference possesses all four required characteristics. In the case of the purely negative (kevalavyatireki) inference, since the probandum (sādhya) is not previously established, its negative pervasion (vyatirekavyāpti) is difficult to grasp; therefore, the purely negative inference is rejected. Furthermore, the capacity of inference to have an entirely supersensible object as its domain is refuted both for the purely positive and the positive-negative (anvayavyatireki) types. Thus, there are two varieties of inference.

Some divide this inference into two types, namely *svārtha* (for oneself) and *parārtha* (for others). Others, however, maintain that since all inferences function by the power of one's own internal synthesis (*pratisaṃdhāna*) and so forth, they serve merely as causes for one's own linguistic usage; thus, they hold that there is only *svārthānumāna*. Regarding inference, some say it consists of five members, having divided it into these two types: *svārtha* and *parārtha*. Others, however, maintain that since all inferences function by the power of one's own internal synthesis and so forth, they serve merely as causes for one's own linguistic usage; thus, they hold that there is only *svārthānumāna*.
Inference consists of five members;

that is, the statement communicating that inference is joined with five members in the form of the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), the example (*udāharaṇa*), the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*). Among these, the statement of the subject (*pakṣa*) as possessing the property to be proved (*sādhya*) is the proposition. For example: "The mountain possesses fire. The statement of the mark (*liṅga*) is the reason. For example: "Because it possesses smoke. The statement of the illustrative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*) preceded by the indication of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is the example. That is of two kinds, according to the distinction between positive (*anvaya*) and negative (*vyatireka*) concomitance.

For example: "Whatever possesses smoke possesses fire, as in a kitchen"—this is the positive instance (*anvayodāharaṇa*). "Whatever is without fire is without smoke, as in a lake"—this is the negative instance (*vyatirekodāharaṇa*). The application (*upanaya*) is the statement that summarizes the reason (*hetu*) in the subject (*pakṣa*) by means of its pervasion (*vyāpti*), based on the consideration of the illustrative examples. It is also of two kinds, according to the distinction between the positive and the negative. "And thus, it possesses smoke" is the positive application (*anvayopanaya*); and "but this [mountain] is not like that, being without smoke" is the negative application (*vyatirekopanaya*).

The conclusion (*nigamana*) is the statement that summarizes the probandum (*sādhya*) within the subject (*pakṣa*), preceded by the reason (*hetu*). This too is of two kinds, exactly like [the previous members]. For example: "Therefore, this [mountain] possesses fire" is the conclusion by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*); "Therefore, this is not without fire" is by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
This demonstrates the difference of opinion among philosophers regarding the scope of the members of inference (*anumāna*).

Thus, the Naiyāyikas maintain that there are five members [of a syllogism]; the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that there are three members, namely the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*udāharaṇa*); and the Buddhists maintain that there are two members, namely the example and the application (*upanaya*). For us, however, there is no fixed rule: sometimes there are five members, sometimes three, and sometimes two. This is because the universal concomitance (*vyāpti*) and the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) are established by the example and the application alone; therefore, an inference is valid with just those two.

The application of discourse through detailed exposition or summary depends on whether one possesses dull, middling, or sharp intelligence; thus, there is no fixed rule. Likewise, only a valid reason (*saddhetu*) endowed with the five members is capable of inferring fire. Because it is called a "valid reason," no inference of fire arises from a mass of dust resembling smoke. These are fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*).

Other fallacies that appear to be reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are those that resemble valid reasons; they are of five types, distinguished as: unestablished (*asiddha*), contradictory (*viruddha*), inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), neutralized by the context (*prakaraṇasama*), and mistimed (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*). Among these, the unestablished is threefold: unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*), unestablished in its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*), and unestablished in its pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddha*). An example of the unestablished in its own nature is: "The living body is non-eternal, because it is visible, like a pot. An example of the unestablished in its locus is: "A lotus in the sky is fragrant, because it is a lotus, like a lotus in a pond."

The locus, the sky-lotus (*vyomāravinda*), is unestablished (*asiddha*). The "unestablished due to the lack of pervasion" (*vyāpyatvāsiddha*) is of two kinds: one due to the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that grasps the pervasion (*vyāpti*), and the other due to the existence of a limiting condition (*upādhi*). The first is, for example: "Whatever exists is momentary. This is because there is no established means of valid cognition to grasp the pervasion between momentariness and existence. The second is, for example: "The killing of an animal dedicated to Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīya-hiṃsā*) is a producer of demerit (*adharma*), because it is a form of killing, like killing outside of a sacrifice (*ṛtu-bāhya-hiṃsā*). Here, "being prohibited" (*niṣiddhatva*) is the limiting condition. Therefore, the reason (*hetu*) "because it is a form of killing" is "vitiated by a limiting condition" (*sopādhika*).

A reason that is pervaded by the opposite of the probandum (*sādhya*) is the contradictory (*viruddha*). For example: "Nature (*prakṛti*) is eternal, because it is produced, like time. Here, the reason "being produced" is pervaded by the absence of the probandum. The inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) is that which deviates [from the probandum]. It is of two kinds: common (*sādhāraṇa*) and uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*). That which occurs in the subject (*pakṣa*), the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), and the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) is the common inconclusive. For example: "Sound is eternal, because it is knowable (*prameyatva*), like time. The uncommon, however, is that which is excluded from both the similar and dissimilar instances.

For example: "Earth is eternal, because it possesses odor, like space. *Prakaraṇasama*, however, is that which possesses another reason (*hetvantara*) that establishes the opposite of the probandum (*sādhya*). For example: "The Lord is eternal, because he is devoid of non-eternal attributes"; [and] "The Lord is not eternal, because he is devoid of eternal attributes. This very [fallacy] is the *satpratipakṣa* (counter-balanced). That reason for which the subject (*pakṣa*) possesses the absence of the probandum is *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (mistimed). For example: "Fire is not hot, because it is a category of object (*padārtha*), like water. And this is sublated (*bādhita*) by the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that determines its heat.
The determination of the inclusion of comparison (*upamāna*) within inference (*anumāna*) and other means of knowledge:

Once inference has been thus defined, the inclusion of comparison and the rest within inference is as follows—Comparison is the cognition of an object qualified by similarity, which is assisted by the recollection of the meaning of a statement of correspondence (*atideśavākya*). For example, one who does not know a *gavaya* hears from a forest-dweller that "a *gavaya* is like a cow. Having gone to the forest and recollecting the meaning of that statement, when he perceives an object qualified by similarity to a cow, the resulting cognition of that object qualified by similarity to a cow—assisted by the recollection of the meaning of the statement—is known as comparison. This is what is called comparison.

Because it consists of the nature of recollection (*smaraṇa*), its inclusion within perception (*pratyakṣa*) [is suggested]; because it depends upon the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*), its inclusion within inference (*anumāna*) [is suggested]; and because it is produced by a sentence, its inclusion within verbal testimony (*śabda*) is also to be inferred.
The manner in which presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) and the others are included within inference is as follows:

Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is the postulation of a person’s eating at night based on observing his corpulence while he does not eat during the day; its inclusion is within inference (*anumāna*). Hypothetical reasoning (*tarka*) is the demonstration of an undesirable consequence regarding the pervader (*vyāpaka*) by accepting the pervaded (*vyāpya*); for example, in the inference "the mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke," when it is said, "let there be smoke, but let there be no fire," [one responds]: "if there were no fire, then there would be no smoke either. Its function is to assist the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Ascertainment (*niścaya*) is the determination of reality preceded by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) assisted by reasoning (*tarka*). Discussion (*vāda*) is a discourse between those free from passion. Disputation (*jalpa*) is a debate for victory characterized by the presentation of proofs for both sides. Futile rejoinder (*jāti*) is a refutation that is self-defeating; or, it is an improper reply. Point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) is the cause of defeat. Since these are auxiliary members of inference, they are included within inference. In some instances, [the terminology] has been stated in accordance with the Nyāya school’s convention; this was stated following their system, and thus there is no contradiction. Thus, inference has been defined.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Exposition of Inference," within the *Śārīrakaparibhāṣā* of the *Yatīndramatadīpikā*, composed by Śrīnivāsadāsa, the foremost disciple of the venerable Mahācārya, the ornament of the Vādhūla lineage.

Now begins the third section. Following the examination of inference, verbal testimony (*śabda*) is examined. Verbal knowledge is the cognition of an object produced by a statement uttered by one who is not untrustworthy (*anāpta*). The instrument (*karaṇa*) of that [knowledge] is the means of valid verbal cognition (*śabdapramāṇa*). By the inclusion of the term "uttered by one who is not untrustworthy," the view that the Veda is of human origin (*pauruṣeya*) is refuted. Alternatively, it may be defined as a statement that is free from defects in its cause and lacks any subverting cognition (*bādhakapratyaya*).

By the statement that at the beginning of creation, the Blessed One, having repeatedly remembered the Vedas as distinguished by their respective prior successions, taught them to the Four-faced One (Brahmā), the eternity and non-human origin of the Veda are established; thus, there is an absence of defects in the cause and an absence of subverting cognition.
This constitutes the demonstration of the authority of the complete Veda.

If it is objected: "Since the Mīmāṃsakas accept the authority of Vedic sentences only on the grounds that they have the nature of *kārya* (what is to be done), and since it is impossible to acquire linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*) regarding sentences whose purport is the already-established (*siddha*) Brahman, how can such sentences possess authority?"—we say no. For even sentences whose purport is the established Brahman are accepted as being connected to a *kārya* in the form of meditation (*upāsanā*). Furthermore, we observe that even a worldly sentence concerning an established fact, such as "Your father is sitting comfortably," possesses the capacity to produce understanding.

In the world, for children, their mothers, fathers, and others point with their fingers to objects such as "mother," "father," "uncle," or "moon," employing words that denote them; thus, the capacity of a word to convey meaning gradually becomes possible, and there is no room for suspicion regarding its lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*). If so, one might ask: how can the portion of the Veda that teaches black magic (*abhicāra*) and the like be authoritative? This is not a valid objection, because by demonstrating visible results, it serves as a motivator for engaging in the means to achieve invisible results such as heaven.

The statement regarding the sacrificial post and the sun (*yūpādityavākya*) is intended to illuminate the sacrificial post as being like the sun; therefore, the authority of the entire Veda is established. This is the division of the Veda.

That Veda is divided into two parts by its preceding and succeeding sections, which respectively establish ritual action (*karman*) and Brahman. The first section (*pūrvakāṇḍa*) establishes the rituals for propitiation; the latter section (*uttarakāṇḍa*) establishes the Brahman that is to be propitiated. Therefore, the two *mīmāṃsās* constitute a single system of study (*ekaśāstrya*). The Veda, consisting of these two parts, is established as fourfold in the form of the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, *Sāma*, and *Atharva* Vedas, and it is further of infinite varieties. The Veda, with its many forms such as the *Ṛk* and others, is threefold in the nature of mantra, arthavāda, and injunction (*vidhi*).

A *mantra* is a statement that illuminates the meaning of what is to be performed. An *arthavāda* is a specific type of sentence that strengthens the inclination toward action prompted by an injunction (*vidhi*). An injunction (*vidhi*) here is a statement in the form of beneficial instruction; it is of three kinds, distinguished as *apūrva* (novel), *parisaṅkhyā* (exclusionary), and *niyama* (restrictive). These, in turn, are manifold according to distinctions such as obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*). "One sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*) is an *apūrva-vidhi*. (The injunction for meditation on the nature of being mind-made, etc., is a *viśiṣṭa-vidhi*.)

The injunction "imām agr̥bhṇan raśanām" is an injunction of exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā-vidhi*). An injunction regarding the non-departure from one's teacher and so forth is an injunction of restriction (*niyama-vidhi*). An injunction regarding the twilight worship (*sandhyopāsana*) and so forth is a mandatory injunction (*nitya-vidhi*). An injunction regarding the *jāteṣṭi* sacrifice and so forth is an occasional injunction (*naimittika-vidhi*). An injunction regarding the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice and so forth is an optional injunction (*kāmya-vidhi*). These are the Vedāṅgas.

Thus, for the Veda—which consists of injunctions (*vidhi*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and mantras—there are these auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*): prosody (*chandas*), ritual science (*kalpa*), phonetics (*śikṣā*), etymology (*nirukta*), astronomy (*jyotiṣa*), and grammar (*vyākaraṇa*). Prosody consists of the exposition of *anuṣṭubh*, *triṣṭubh*, and other meters. Ritual science is devoted to the exposition of the application of Śrauta and Smārta rites. Phonetics consists of the determination of phonemes. Etymology explains words whose meanings are not otherwise known. Astronomy determines the times for study and the performance of those rites.

Grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), however, is primarily concerned with the justification of correct words, accents, and so forth. Thus, the authority of the Veda, together with its auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga*), is established. Now, regarding the investigation of the authority of the Smṛtis and other texts: the Smṛti—composed by authoritative persons (*āpta*) and teaching conduct, customary practice, expiation (*prāyaścitta*), and so on that is not contradicted by the Śruti—is authoritative. Although Hiraṇyagarbha and others are authoritative, because they are subject to the influence of the three *guṇas*, only those portions of the Smṛtis composed by them (such as those of Yoga and Kapila) which do not contradict the Smṛtis of Manu and others are authoritative. Those portions that contradict reality through errors such as the inversion of principles (*tattva-viparyāsa*) are not authoritative.

Those portions that are contrary to reality, such as those involving error and the like, are not authoritative. Furthermore, the authority of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, which serve to supplement the Vedas, is self-evident. In this regard, although contradictions may occasionally appear in the Bhārata and Rāmāyaṇa, they should be interpreted as being non-contradictory with respect to their essential truth, just like the statements of the Vedānta.

Even among the Purāṇas that expound the five topics beginning with creation (*sarga*), which are divided into *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa* categories, there is no contradiction regarding the portion concerning the ultimate reality (*tattva*); thus, while the contradictory portions are not authoritative, everything else is authoritative. The same applies to the Āgamas of the Pāśupatas and others. As for the venerable Pāñcarātra Āgama, which is distinguished by various divisions such as Āgama, Divya, Tantra, and Tantrāntara Siddhānta, it possesses authority in its entirety because there is no contradiction with the Veda anywhere within it. The same is true for the Vaikhānasa Āgama as well. The Dharmaśāstras are likewise [authoritative].

Śāṇḍilya, Parāśara, Bharadvāja, Vasiṣṭha, Hārīta, and others are the authors of the Dharmaśāstras. Likewise, the arts (śilpa), Ayurveda, Gāndharva, the Bharata-āgama, and so forth, are authoritative in their respective applicable portions. "Art" (śilpa) refers to that which teaches agriculture and the like, as well as the construction of city gates, ramparts, and so on. Ayurveda is medicine. Gāndharva is that which defines singing and the like. The Bharata-āgama is that which prescribes dance and other such performances. Furthermore, within the treatises on the sixty-four arts, there are authorities useful for the principles, the means, and the goals of human life. This constitutes the demonstration of the authority of the *Sahasragīti* and the *Śrībhāṣya*.

The divine compositions of the great teachers, such as Bakula and others, beginning with the *Śrīsūktas*, are authoritative in their entirety. The treatises composed by Śrīmad Rāmānujācārya and others, such as the *Śrībhāṣya*, are the most authoritative.
[This concludes] the investigation of the *Vākya* and other [works].

That which is characterized by a specific composition dependent upon human independence is "pauruṣeya" (human-made). By this, the definition of poetry, drama, rhetoric, and so forth, is also stated. Likewise, worldly sentences uttered by a reliable person (*āpta*), possessing expectancy, semantic competency, and proximity, are also means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). For example: "There are five fruits on the bank of the river," and so on. Thus, the sentence common to both Vedic and worldly usage is of two kinds, distinguished by primary function (*mukhyavṛtti*) and secondary function (*gauṇavṛtti*). Primary function is the function of direct denotation (*abhidhāvṛtti*).

For example, the word "lion" refers to the king of beasts; that primary denotative function (*abhidhā-vṛtti*) is of many kinds, such as through etymological derivation (*yoga*), conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), and so forth. When the primary meaning is obstructed, the function [of a word] toward a meaning proximate to it is metaphorical (*aupacārika*). That is twofold, due to the distinction between indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and secondary implication (*gauṇī*). The first is, for example, in the phrase "a hamlet on the Ganges," where because the [literal] sense of location is obstructed, there is indication with respect to the bank.

The second is, for example, in the phrase "Devadatta is a lion," where [the term applies] to Devadatta due to his connection with qualities such as valor. Thus, every collection of sentences, whether Vedic or worldly, has as its object that which possesses distinctions and that which consists of difference.

Just as words denoting the body find their ultimate referent in the embodied soul, so too do words denoting conscious beings such as Brahmā, Rudra, Agni, Indra, and others—who constitute the body of the Blessed Lord—find their ultimate referent in Him; and likewise, words denoting unconscious entities such as primordial nature (prakṛti), time, space, and vital breath—which also constitute His body—find their ultimate referent in the embodied soul. Thus, both the words denoting the conscious beings who are the body of the Blessed Lord and the words denoting the unconscious entities that are His body find their final convergence in the embodied soul.

The Teachers establish that the ultimate culmination [of all inquiry] lies in Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Self. It has been stated that through the knowledge of Vedānta, one's proficiency reaches fulfillment. We shall, however, demonstrate in the subsequent section on the Lord (Īśvara-pariccheda) how Nārāyaṇa is denotable by all words, possesses all things as His body, and so forth. Thus, the word (*śabda*) has been defined. Thus ends the third chapter, titled "Definition of the Word," in the *Śārīrakaparibhāṣā* within the *Yatīndramatadīpikā*, composed by Śrīnivāsadāsa, the first disciple of the venerable Mahācārya, the ornament of the Vādhūla lineage. Now begins the fourth chapter.
The establishment of the twofold division of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) into substance (*dravya*) and non-substance (*adravya*).

Following the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the object of knowledge is now defined. That which is most excellently measured is the *prameya*. It is of two kinds, due to the distinction between substance and non-substance. Substance is the material cause (*upādāna*). The material cause is that which is the substratum of states (*avasthā*). If it be asked: "Since other schools enumerate seven categories (*padārtha*)—substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, inherence, and absence—how can it be established as twofold through the division of substance and non-substance? It is said in reply:

If one were to postulate that action (*karman*) exists in five ways—namely, as distinguished by upward throwing, downward throwing, contraction, expansion, and locomotion—that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*); for it is more appropriate to establish action as being of a single nature, consisting essentially of motion. Furthermore, even in that case, [the classification] is established simply by taking conjunction (*saṃyoga*) into account. As for the universal (*jāti*), since we do not admit a universal over and above its configuration (*saṃsthāna*), configuration itself is the universal. Likewise, regarding inherence (*samavāya*), because there would be an infinite regress if another inherence were admitted, we do not admit a universal over and above it.

If one were to accept another inherence (*samavāya*) within inherence itself, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), since that too could be accounted for by its being a qualifier of a conjoined entity. Furthermore, it is cumbersome (*gaurava*) to accept some category called "particularity" (*viśeṣa*) apart from the distinguishing properties such as atomicity and omnipresence that differentiate the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*). Moreover, because action (*karman*), generality (*sāmānya*), particularity (*viśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*) are not accepted as separate categories, the twofold division into "substance" (*dravya*) and "non-substance" (*adravya*) is logically established.

By this, the claim that "non-existence" (*abhāva*) is a seventh category (*padārtha*) is also refuted, because non-existence is essentially a form of another existence (*bhāvāntara*). Prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is a succession of prior states; destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) is a succession of subsequent states; and absolute and mutual non-existence (*atyantānyonyābhāva*) are simply the specific natures (*svarūpa*) residing in other substrates (*dharmin*). Its inclusion within perception (*pratyakṣa*) has been stated previously. It was stated that substance (*dravya*) is the material cause (*upādāna*); furthermore, the general definition of substance as "that which is the locus of qualities" (*guṇāśraya*) is also possible.

And those substances are six, distinguished as: primordial nature (*prakṛti*), time (*kāla*), pure being (*sattva*), the elements (*bhūta*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*). Among these, between the two distinct categories of the insentient (*jaḍa*) and the sentient (*ajaḍa*), the definition of the insentient is stated: "The insentient is that which is devoid of unmixed *sattva*. That [insentient] is of two kinds, through the distinction between primordial nature and time. Herein follows the description of primordial nature (*prakṛti*).

In this context, *prakṛti* is that which has the nature of being the substratum for the three *guṇas*—*sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. It is eternal, imperishable, and designated by such terms as *vidyā* and *māyā*. Its state of being oriented toward manifestation (*kāryonmukhāvasthā*), resulting from an imbalance of the *guṇas* dependent upon the will of the Lord, is denoted by the term *avyakta* (the unmanifest). From that, the *mahat* (the Great Principle) arises. That *mahat* exists in three forms, distinguished as *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa*. From the *mahat*, the *ahaṃkāra* (ego) arises; it too becomes threefold: *sāttvika-ahaṃkāra*, *rājasa-ahaṃkāra*, and *tāmasa-ahaṃkāra*.

These three also have other names: vaikārika, taijasa, and bhūtādi. Among them, from the sāttvika ahaṃkāra—well-known as *vaikārika* and assisted by the rājasa ahaṃkāra designated as *taijasa*—the eleven organs are born.
This is the definition of the organs.

The definition of a sense organ (*indriya*) is: a substance whose material cause (*upādāna*) is the *sāttvika* ego (*ahaṅkāra*). The sense organs are of two kinds: the organs of cognition (*jñānendriya*) and the organs of action (*karmendriya*). An organ of cognition is a sense organ capable of the extension of knowledge. It is sixfold, distinguished as mind (*manas*), ear, eye, nose, tongue, and skin. The mind is the organ that effects memory and so forth; it resides in the region of the heart and is denoted by such terms as intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and consciousness (*citta*); furthermore, it is the cause of both bondage and liberation.

Among the five [objects] beginning with sound, the sense organ capable of perceiving sound alone is the auditory faculty (*śrotra*); in humans and others it resides within the cavity of the ear, while in snakes and similar creatures it resides in the eye. Likewise, the sense organ capable of perceiving form alone is the visual faculty (*cakṣus*), which in all beings resides in the eye. The sense organ capable of perceiving odor alone is the olfactory faculty (*ghrāṇa*), which resides at the tip of the nose (in elephants and others, it resides at the tip of the trunk). The sense organ capable of perceiving taste alone is the gustatory faculty (*rasana*), which resides at the tip of the tongue.

The tactile organ (*tvagindriya*) is that sense-organ capable of apprehending mere touch; it pervades the entire body, though touch is not perceived in the nails, teeth, hair, and so forth, due to the varying degrees of the vitality of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). The demonstration that the auditory and other organs are elemental (*bhautika*) is merely figurative, based on their being nourished by the elements. According to the tradition of the elders, the connection of these organs with their objects is, in some cases, conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and in others, inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktāśrayaṇa*). The general definition of the organs of action (*karmendriya*) is the capacity for any one of the actions such as speaking and the rest.

And that [organ] exists in five forms, distinguished as speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals. Speech is the organ that effects the utterance of phonemes; it resides in eight locations consisting of the heart, throat, root of the tongue, palate, teeth, lips, nose, and head. Its absence in [the species] such as deer and the mute is due to the absence of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). The hand is the organ that effects manual craft; it resides at the tips of the fingers in humans and the like, and at the tip of the trunk in elephants and the like. The foot is the organ that effects locomotion.

And that [organ] resides in the feet and so forth of humans and others; it resides in the chest, wings, and so forth of serpents, birds, and others. The organ that effects the discharge of waste is the anus; it resides in those respective parts. The organ that produces specific pleasure is the generative organ (upastha); it resides in the penis and so forth. These organs are atomic (aṇu) in size; they travel along with the individual soul (jīva) during entry into another body, transition to other worlds, and similar states.

In the state of liberation, because the senses cannot travel to a non-material realm, they remain right here until the final dissolution (pralaya), or else they are sustained by others who are devoid of physical organs. The position that the organs of action perish with the destruction of the body must be rejected, as it contradicts the Bhāṣya and other authoritative texts. By this, various dissenting views—such as the existence of a male organ or female organ, the doctrine of a single sense-organ, or the acceptance of the skin as the sole sense-organ—are refuted.
[This concludes] the description of the five subtle elements (tanmātras) and the five gross elements (bhūtas).

From the *tāmasa* ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), designated as *bhūtādi*, which is conjoined with the *rājasa* ego-sense, the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*)—sound and the rest—and the five gross elements (*mahābhūtas*)—ether and the rest—are produced. A *tanmātra* is a substance characterized by the immediate, subtle state of the elements; it is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the elements. An element (*bhūta*) is the substratum for specific objects such as sound and the rest. The subtle elements are five: the subtle element of sound, the subtle element of touch, the subtle element of form, the subtle element of taste, and the subtle element of smell.
The gross elements are likewise five, distinguished as ether, air, fire, water, and earth.
The Description of Space (*ākāśa*):

In this context, the substance characterized by an intermediate state between the *tāmasa-ahaṃkāra* and space is the sound-tanmātra (*śabda-tanmātra*), like the transformation of the turbid state between milk and curd. From that, space is born. The definition of space is: being the substratum of a specific sound while lacking touch, and being the nourisher of the sense of hearing (*śrotra*). It possesses the quality of sound alone and is the cause of providing room (*avakāśa*). It is perceptible through direct perception, as evidenced by the cognition "the sky is blue."

By means of the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*), that [ether] possesses parts and form; by this, the non-produced nature of ether is refuted. Since the conventional usage of "east" and so forth is established through ether itself as conjoined with the movement of the sun (*sūryaparispanda*), there is no need to postulate "direction" (*dik*) as a separate substance. The creation of direction, however, is established in the same manner as the creation of the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) and other elements. [Now follows] the description of air (*vāyu*).

From space arises the subtle element of touch (*sparśatanmātra*). The subtle element of touch is a substance characterized by an intermediate state between space and air. From that, air arises. The definition of air is: being devoid of color while possessing a specific quality of touch; being a substance perceptible solely by the sense organ of touch belonging to beings such as ourselves; and being devoid of color while possessing a specific touch that is neither hot nor cold. In that [air], the designations "cold," "hot," or "fragrant" arise due to contact with various components such as water, sunlight, or flowers.

And it (the body) assists by nourishing the sense-organ of touch (*tvagindriya*). Its qualities (*guṇa*) are sound and touch. Among these, *prāṇa* is a specific type of air (*vāyu*) that is the cause for maintaining the body and so forth. It is of five kinds, distinguished as *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *vyāna*, *udāna*, and *samāna*. The rule that *prāṇa* is in the heart, *apāna* in the anus, *vyāna* pervades the entire body, *udāna* is in the throat, and *samāna* is in the region of the navel applies only to mobile beings. In immobile beings, however, there exists only the nature of connection with *prāṇa*. Since air is perceptible through touch, the claim that it is merely inferable is refuted. [Now follows] the description of fire (*tejas*).
The substance characterized by a state intermediate between air and fire is the subtle element of form (rūpa-tanmātra); from that, fire arises.

The definition of fire (*tejas*) consists in possessing a hot touch, possessing a luminous form, and so forth. Its function as the cause of external cooking and the like occurs in the form of fire (*agni*) and the sun (*sūrya*); internally, it exists in the form of the digestive fire known as *vaiśvānara*. Furthermore, for those other than the owl (*divābhīta*), it serves as an auxiliary factor through the medium of light in visual perception. It is fourfold: terrestrial (*bhauma*), celestial (*divya*), digestive (*audarya*), and mineral (*ākaraja*). Among these, terrestrial fire is that which has earth alone as its fuel, such as a lamp and the like. Celestial fire is that which has water alone as its fuel, such as the sun and the like.

[Fire] is of four kinds: that which has water, earth, or fuel as its substrate; that which is internal, such as the digestive fire (*jāṭhara*); and that which is without a substrate, such as gold produced from a mine. The absence of the sensation of heat in gold is due to its contact with other substances. Furthermore, light (*prabhā*) and that which possesses light (*prabhāvat*) are distinguished in general. Light is a specific manifestation of fire characterized by contraction, expansion, or diffusion, depending on the presence or absence of an obstruction. By this, the view that light is merely a quality (*guṇa*) is refuted. That which is qualified by light is "that which possesses light. It has been established that it is of four kinds. And that fire possesses the qualities of sound, touch, and color.

The definition of water (*ap*) is: a substance characterized by a state intermediate between fire and water, consisting of the subtle element of taste (*rasa-tanmātra*). From that [subtle element], water arises. Possessing cold touch, being devoid of smell, and possessing a specific taste—these and other such qualities constitute the definition of water. Although these [atoms of water] possess a single nature that is white, sweet, and cold, there is an imposition of diversity in color, taste, and touch due to differences in contact with their substrates and other factors. They exist in many forms, such as oceans, rivers, and so forth, and possess the qualities of sound, touch, form, and taste. Furthermore, they are the causes of moistening, coagulation, and other such effects. This concludes the definition of earth.

The substance characterized by an intermediate state between water and earth is the subtle element of smell (*gandhatanmātra*). From that, earth arises. The definition of earth is: possessing a specific odor, and, while possessing taste, possessing a touch that is neither hot nor cold, and so forth. It is fragrant, sweet, black in color, and possesses a touch that is neither hot nor cold. Due to the difference in cooking (*pākabheda*), it possesses various colors, odors, and tastes; it benefits [beings] by nourishing the mind and the sense of smell. It exists in many forms, such as clay, stone, food, medicinal herbs, and the like.

Earth possesses the qualities of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, and it is the cause of support. Darkness is included within earth because it possesses those same qualities or because it is a particular state of it. For this very reason, positions such as "darkness is merely the absence of light and not a distinct substance" are refuted.
[This concludes] the exposition of the process of quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa).

In all elements, the qualities such as sound and the rest are perceived through the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*). As for the process of quintuplication: having created the elements, the Lord divides each single element into two parts; having set aside one part as its own nature, He divides the other part into four. He then joins those four parts with the four other elements.

Thus, when all the elements are being processed, half of each individual element constitutes its own portion (*svabhāga*), while the other half is a collection of portions from the other four elements. Consequently, because one's own portion is greater and the portion of others is smaller, there arises the designation of "earth" and so forth. Furthermore, the instruction on "trivṛtkaraṇa" (threefold processing) found in the Veda is also indicative of *pañcīkaraṇa* (fivefold processing). Some also say that when the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*) combine with the elements, it is called "saptīkaraṇa" (sevenfold processing).

Among these twenty-four principles, the five elements, primordial matter (*prakṛti*), the great one (*mahat*), and the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) are the material causes of the body. The eleven organs, each being innumerable and distinct for every individual soul, remain pervading the body like jewels set in a crown.
This is the definition of the body.

The first definition is that the body is a specific substance that exists as non-distinct from consciousness by way of the constraints of being supported, being controlled, and being subordinate. Alternatively, the three definitions may be applied as follows: that which is necessarily supported, that which is necessarily controlled, and that which is necessarily subordinate. Or, the extrinsic definition (taṭastha-lakṣaṇa) is: a substance other than God and His knowledge. By this [definition], the body is the substratum of movement; the body is the substratum of the sense organs; and the body is the locus of experience.
The definitions of the body propounded by others—such as "the body consists of the head, hands, feet, and so forth"—have been refuted.

The classification of the body is as follows: the body is of two kinds, eternal (*nitya*) and non-eternal (*anitya*). Among these, the eternal body is the body of the Lord (*Īśvara*), which consists of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), substance, time, the individual soul (*jīva*), the substratum of auspiciousness (*śubhāśraya*), and so on; it also includes the natural forms of the eternal sages (*sūris*), such as Garuḍa, the serpent, and others. The non-eternal body is of two kinds: that produced by karma and that not produced by karma. The first is the form of the Great Principle (*mahat*) and so forth belonging to the Lord. Likewise, there are the various forms assumed at will by Ananta, Garuḍa, and other liberated souls (*muktas*), as well as by the Lord himself.

That which is produced by karma is also twofold: that produced by one's own volitional action (*saṅkalpa*) and that produced by mere action (*kevala-karma*). The former belongs to great beings such as Saubhari and others; the latter belongs to others. Furthermore, in general, it is twofold according to the distinction between the immobile (*sthāvara*) and the mobile (*jaṅgama*). The immobile are stones, trees, shrubs, and so forth. The mobile are fourfold, according to the distinction between gods, humans, animals, and denizens of hell. The distinctions of being born from a sprout, from sweat, from an egg, and from a womb are also classifying attributes. There are also bodies not born from a womb (*ayonija*). This concludes the determination of the relationship between cause and effect regarding the creation of the cosmic aggregate (*samaṣṭi-sṛṣṭi*).

Thus, it is precisely the fivefold-compounded elements (*pañcīkṛtabhūta*) that produce the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*). The creation prior to the production of the egg is the collective creation (*samaṣṭisṛṣṭi*); the creation immediately following is the individual creation (*vyaṣṭisṛṣṭi*). The so-called "production" of the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest is merely the attainment of a different state, according to the maxim of the palm leaf, the palāśa leaf, and the chisel. Just as with the conventional usage of terms such as "army," "forest," or "heap," the distinction between cause and effect exists merely through the connection of specific preceding and succeeding states.

In this regard, the designation of a distinct principle (*tattva*) occurs only up to the earth element, upon reaching a state of a different kind through the abandonment of the prior state. Thus, twenty-four principles have been described according to the division of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the great one (*mahat*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), the eleven organs, the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), and the five gross elements (*bhūta*). By this, those outsiders who maintain a number of principles either less or more than this are refuted; likewise, the Pāśupatas and those who maintain that atoms are the cause are also refuted.
[Now follows] the description of Jambūdvīpa.

Prakṛti and the others constitute the objects of enjoyment, the instruments of enjoyment, and the places of enjoyment for both the Lord and the individual soul (*jīva*). The objects of enjoyment are the sense-objects; the instruments of enjoyment are the organs such as the eyes; and the places of enjoyment are the cosmic eggs (*aṇḍa*) together with the fourteen worlds. A "cosmic egg" is a material substance derived from *prakṛti*, composed of the five gross elements (*pañcīkṛta-pañcabhūta*), and shaped like a wood-apple (*kapittha-phala*). For example: the earth is shaped like a lotus, and Mount Meru is shaped like its pericarp. To the south of Meru are three regions; in front is the region of Bhadrāśva; behind is the region of Ketumāla; and in the center is Ilāvṛta.
Thus is the description of the earth consisting of seven islands:

Jambūdvīpa, endowed with nine regions, is one hundred thousand yojanas in extent and is surrounded by the salt ocean of equal measure. That ocean is encircled by Plakṣadvīpa, which consists of seven regions and is twice the size [of the preceding]. That too is surrounded by the sugarcane ocean (Ikṣurasoda). That sea is surrounded by Śālmalidvīpa; that again by the wine ocean (Surāsoda); that by Kuśadvīpa; that by the clarified butter ocean (Sarpisoda); and that too by Krauñcadvīpa; and that by the curd ocean (Vadhyasoma).

That [Plakṣadvīpa] is surrounded by Śākadvīpa; that by the Ocean of Milk; and that by Puṣkaradvīpa, which is shaped like a circle dividing two regions and contains the Mānasottara mountain. That [Puṣkaradvīpa] is surrounded by the Ocean of Pure Water. In this manner, each successive continent should be understood to be double the size of the preceding one. The five continents beginning with Plakṣadvīpa consist of seven regions (*varṣas*). This [Puṣkaradvīpa], consisting of two continents, is encircled by a golden land twice its size. That golden land is surrounded by the Lokāloka mountain.
That mountain is surrounded by darkness, the darkness by the waters of the pit, and those by the shell of the cosmic egg (*aṇḍakaṭāha*).

Thus, below the earth, there are seven worlds distinguished as Atala, Vitala, Nitala, Talātala, Mahātala, Sutala, and Pātāla. Below these are the hells; they are the realms for the experience of the fruits of evil deeds by those of sinful karma, such as Raurava and others, and primarily consist of twenty-one divisions. Beyond that is darkness (Tamas), beyond that is Gartodaka, and beyond that is the shell of the cosmic egg (Aṇḍakaṭāha).
This concludes the description of the extent of the region above the earth.

Thus, one hundred thousand *yojanas* above the earth is the solar orb (*sūryamaṇḍala*). That much constitutes the *bhuvarloka*. Above that is the lunar orb (*candramaṇḍala*). Above that, in ascending order, are the orbs of the constellations, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, and the Seven Sages (*saptarṣi*). Above those is the Pole Star (*dhruva*). From the solar orb up to the world of the Pole Star is the *svarloka*. One million four hundred thousand *yojanas* above that is the *maharloka*, which is one crore *yojanas* in height. The *janoloka* is twice that size. The *tapoloka* is four times that.

Therefore, Satyaloka is twelve crores [of yojanas] in height. Beyond that are the darkness, the pit, and the eggshell. Thus, by measuring across and upwards, the extent of the earth is said to be fifty crores of yojanas. The doctrine of its being one hundred crores of yojanas in width is due to a difference in measurement. The eggshell is one crore of yojanas in height. This concludes the fourth incarnation.

That egg is enveloped by ten successive coverings. There are infinite such eggs, created simultaneously by the Lord like bubbles upon water. It is the discernment that the creation of the Lord up to the four-faced Brahmā is without intermediaries (advārikā), whereas after that, it is with intermediaries (sadvārikā). The detailed account should be seen in the *Purāṇaratna* and other such works. Thus, Prakṛti has been described.

Thus ends the fourth incarnation, titled "The Exposition of Primordial Nature" (*prakṛtinirūpaṇa*), within the *Yatīndramatadīpikā*, a glossary of the *Śārīraka* [Brahma-sūtras], composed by Śrīnivāsadāsa, the ornament of the illustrious Vādhūla lineage and the primary recipient of the grace of the venerable Great Teacher.

Now begins the fifth descent: the determination of time (*kāla*). Next, time, which is a specific insentient entity, is defined. Time is a particular insentient substance devoid of the three qualities (*guṇa*). It is eternal and all-pervading. It is threefold, distinguished as past, future, and present. It is the cause for designations such as "simultaneous," "quick," and "long. It is also the cause for the conventional usage of *nimeṣa*, *kāṣṭhā*, *tatparā*, *vināḍī*, *kalā*, *ghaṭikā*, *muhūrta*, day, fortnight (*pakṣa*), month, season (*ṛtu*), solstice (*ayana*), year, and so forth. A month by human reckoning is a single day for the ancestors (*pitṛs*); for them, the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) is midday.

A year by human reckoning is a single day for the gods; for them, the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) is midday, and the [subsequent] period is night. Thus, by the reckoning of the gods, a cycle of four ages (*caturyuga*) is said to consist of twelve thousand years. Among these, the Kṛta Yuga consists of four thousand years, in which Dharma is complete. The Tretā Yuga consists of three thousand years, in which Dharma possesses three quarters. The Dvāpara Yuga is measured at two thousand years, possessing two quarters of Dharma.

The Kali Yuga consists of one thousand years and is endowed with one quarter of Dharma; the transition (sandhi) between these [ages] is two thousand years in number. A period of four thousand such cycles of four ages constitutes the measure of a day of Brahmā. His night is likewise. This is the description of a day of Brahmā.

In a single day of Brahmā, there are fourteen Manus, as well as six Indras and seven groups of Saptarṣis. For each Manu, the duration of time consisting of four yugas passes once. Thus, by the measure of Brahmā, the lifespan of Brahmā is one hundred years. All of this is dependent upon Time (kāla). Likewise, the periodic dissolutions (pralayas)—whether daily, occasional, or primordial—are also dependent on Time. Time is its own material cause (upādāna) with respect to its own effects. Undivided Time is eternal; divided times, however, are transitory.

Time in such a state becomes an accessory for the sport (*krīḍā*) of the Lord. In the realm of the Lord's sportive manifestation (*līlā-vibhūti*), the Lord performs His work entirely dependent upon time. In the eternal manifestation (*nitya-vibhūti*), however, although time exists, it possesses no independence. Some say that time does not exist at all; others claim that time is the Great Principle (*mahat*) characterized by darkness (*tāmasa*). Both of these views are contradicted by scripture (*āgama*) and by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). The Teachers maintain that time is perceivable by the six senses; by this, the proponents of inference (*anumeyavādin*) are refuted. Thus, time has been defined.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Time," in the *Yatīndramatadīpikā*, a treatise on the technical terminology of the Śārīraka [Mīmāṃsā], composed by Śrīnivāsadāsa, the first disciple of the illustrious Mahācārya, the ornament of the Vādhūla lineage.

Now begins the sixth incarnation: the description of the eternal manifestation (*nityavibhūti*). Next, the eternal manifestation is described. The common characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of pure being (*śuddhasattva*), the attribute-knowledge (*dharmabhūtajñāna*), and the individual soul (*jīva*) as well as the Lord (*īśvara*) is non-inertness (*ajaḍatva*). Non-inertness means self-luminosity (*svayamprakāśatva*). Among these, the common characteristic of pure being and attribute-knowledge is non-inertness conditioned by extroversion (*parāktva*). That, however, consists in being manifest only to another while being self-luminous. Pure being (*śuddhasattva*) is the state of possessing *sattva* while being distinct from the substance consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇadravya*).

Alternatively, it is the state of being other than the dissimilar spatial locations where ignorance has been entirely removed. That manifestation is infinite in its upward direction, yet limited in its downward direction. It is insentient, yet self-luminous. Because it brings about bliss, it is of the nature of bliss (*ānanda*). Because it is expounded by the mantras of the five Upaniṣads, it is of the nature of the five Upaniṣads. And because it possesses five non-material powers, it is described as "consisting of the five powers" (*pañcaśaktimayī*).

That manifestation (*vibhūti*) of the Lord consists of objects of enjoyment, instruments of enjoyment, and places of enjoyment, arising from the will of the Lord for both the eternal beings (*nityas*) and the liberated (*muktas*). The objects of enjoyment are the bodies of the Lord and others; the instruments of enjoyment are sandalwood, flowers, garments, ornaments, weapons, and so forth; while the places of enjoyment consist of gate-towers, walls, pavilions, celestial chariots (*vimāna*), gardens, lotus ponds, and the like.
