Among these, the bodies of the Lord and the eternally liberated ones are established by the eternal will of the Blessed One.

The bodies of liberated souls, the creation of their fathers and so forth, the simultaneous assumption of multiple bodies, and other such phenomena occur solely through the will (*saṅkalpa*) of the Blessed Lord. The bodies of the Blessed Lord—whether as the *vyūha*, *vibhava*, or *arcāvatāra*—are non-material (*aprākṛta*). One should not raise the doubt as to how there can be a conjunction of the material and the non-material in the case of *arcāvatāras*; the resolution should be seen according to authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*), just as in the case of the bodies of incarnations such as Śrī Rāma and Kṛṣṇa. This concludes the demonstration of the divine nature of the eternal manifestation (*nityavibhūti*).

As for the assumption of a body and so forth by the liberated, it is indeed service (*kaiṅkarya*), because—just like assuming a costume during a spring festival—it serves as a cause for the expansion of the Master’s countenance. Because the Lord’s body manifests the sixfold attributes (*ṣāḍguṇya*), it is conventionally designated as "the sixfold attributes. The qualities of His divine, auspicious form include eternal, faultless, unsurpassed brilliance, beauty, fragrance, delicacy, charm, youthfulness, softness, and straightforwardness. His all-pervasiveness is well-known in the *Gītā*.

The statement that "the liberated one has no body" refers specifically to the absence of a body produced by karma. In that state, because the senses and other faculties are eternal, and precisely because there is no relationship of cause and effect, they are not designated as distinct principles (*tattva*) as they are in the case of *prakṛti*. By this, the view that the body and so forth do not exist there is refuted. By the expression "beyond darkness," the doctrine that [the liberated state] is merely a portion of *prakṛti* is refuted. Because it is the substratum of non-material (non-*prākṛta*) sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, it is distinguished from space (*ākāśa*).
And by the demonstration that its essence is knowledge, the view that it is insentient (*jaḍa*) is refuted.

The demonstration that the Lord’s divine, auspicious form is the substratum of all: the Lord’s extraordinary, divine, and auspicious form possesses the quality of being the substratum for all principles (*tattva*), as described in the chapter on weapons and ornaments. For example: Puruṣa is the form of the Kaustubha gem; Prakṛti is the form of the Śrīvatsa mark; Mahat is the form of the mace; the Sāttvika-ahaṅkāra is the form of the conch; the Tāmasa-ahaṅkāra is the form of the Śārṅga bow; knowledge is the form of the sword; ignorance is the form of its sheath; and the mind is the form of the discus.

The sense organs and organs of action constitute the body; the subtle and gross elements take the form of a forest garland. Herein, consciousness is the discus, volition is the sword, and the intellect is the sheath for that [sword]; the garland is the covering of the mind.
The elements, through their own qualities, along with the pair of ego-sense and the shell, act as the Śārṅga bow.

O Lord of Kamalā! The wise declare that your arrows are the ten sense-voids, the Kaustubha gem is the individual soul (jīva), the Śrīvatsa mark is the primordial matter (pradhāna), and your mace is the Great Illusion (māyā).

Thus, the verse summarized above should be reflected upon. That manifestation (*vibhūti*) is fourfold, consisting of the forms known as Āmoda, Pramoda, Sammoda, and Vaikuṇṭha. Furthermore, it is infinite, designated by such terms as Tripādvibhūti, Paramapada, Paramavyoma, Paramākāśa, Amṛtanāka, Aprākṛtaloka, Ānandaloka, Vaikuṇṭha, Ayodhyā, and so forth. Within that manifestation is the city named Vaikuṇṭha, endowed with twelve enclosures and surrounded by numerous gate-towers (*gopura*) and ramparts. Therein lies the divine abode named Ānanda.

At its end is the assembly hall known as Mahāmaṇimaṇḍapa, constructed with many thousands of pillars made of jewels. In it resides Ananta, resplendent with the luster of the jewels on his thousand hoods. Upon him is a divine lion-throne composed of Dharma and other virtues. Above that is an eight-petaled lotus being served by Vimalā and others, who hold chowries in their hands. Above that is Śeṣa, the abode of supreme knowledge. Above him is the Great and Supreme Word (Vāk). Thus, the eternal manifestation has been described in brief.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Eternal Glory," in the *Yatīndramatadīpikā*, a treatise on the technical terminology of the Śārīraka [Mīmāṃsā], composed by Śrīnivāsadāsa, the first disciple of the illustrious Mahācārya, the ornament of the Vādhūla lineage.
Now begins the seventh chapter: the characteristics and other attributes of knowledge as the nature of dharma.

Now, the nature of knowledge as an attribute (*dharmabhūta*) is described in its proper order. Its definition is: being an object-possessor while being self-luminous and insentient substance; or, while being all-pervading, being of the nature of a substance and its qualities like light, and being the manifestation of objects—this is what is called "intellect" (*buddhi*). This attribute-knowledge is eternally permanent for both God and the liberated souls.

It is all-pervasive. For those who are bound, it is concealed; for those who are liberated, that which was previously concealed has subsequently become manifest. If it is asked: "If knowledge is eternal, how is the conventional usage 'knowledge has arisen' or 'knowledge has perished' possible?"—it is said in response: this is possible by taking into account the states of contraction and expansion of knowledge. Just as water flows out from a leather bag through its feet [or openings], so too knowledge, having issued forth through the door of the senses, comes into contact with the object. Its contraction and expansion are like those of a coiled or expanded serpent. All knowledge is intrinsically valid (*svataḥ-pramāṇa*) and self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*).

All knowledge is valid by itself and is self-luminous. Consciousness, as it is understood by those who disagree [with this view], is independent in its capacity to produce its own internal linguistic usage, because it is the cause of such usage without depending on a relation with anything of its own kind, just like an object, a sense organ, or a lamp. Furthermore, there is no homogeneity between the eye and light, because they differ in being derived from ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkārika*) and being composed of fire (*taijasa*), respectively.

By this, the following positions are refuted: the momentariness of cognition; its persistence for three moments; the falsity of even the empirical (vyāvahārika) level—just like the apparent (prātibhāsika)—on the grounds that it is sublated; the extrinsic validity (*parataḥ prāmāṇya*) of knowledge; and the identity of cognition itself with the Self (*ātman*). Furthermore, a continuous stream of cognitions such as "pillar, pillar, pillar" is in fact a single cognition. As for the permanence of cognition, the states of waking and so forth are thereby established.

[Objection: But surely, if the eternality of knowledge is accepted on the strength of scripture (*āgama*), how can the distinction between waking, deep sleep, and so forth be established? [Reply: This is not so. Just as there is an absence of burning from fire—which is inherently a burner—due to the presence of an obstructing agent such as a magnet when in proximity to the combustible object, likewise, the establishment of sleep and other states occurs due to the presence of specific forms of darkness (*tamas*) that conceal knowledge. It is also like the nature of manhood (*puṃstva*) and so forth; for manhood and the like, though concealed in childhood, become manifest in youth.

Furthermore, since the definition of a quality (*guṇa*) is "that which has the nature of being dependent upon something else is a quality of that thing," knowledge is a quality because it is characterized by this definition of a quality, just like attributes such as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).

The establishment of knowledge as a substance (*dravya*) is as follows: because it possesses states of contraction and expansion, it is therefore also a substance. One should not question how knowledge, which is an attribute (*guṇa*) of the self, can be a substance; for, as in the case of light, there is no contradiction between being a substance and being an attribute. Indeed, the definition of a substance is that which is the substratum of states. Furthermore, its existence elsewhere than in its own substratum is possible, just as in the case of light. And the formal argument (*prayoga*) is: cognition, though an attribute, is a substance, because it possesses qualities such as diffusion, like light.

Knowledge is a substance because, while being distinct from conjunction and unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), it is a cause of mental impression (bhāvanā), like the self. The simultaneous conjunction of liberated knowledge with infinite locations is possible, like the light of the eyes or the sun.

Knowledge (*jñāna*), intellect (*mati*), wisdom (*prajñā*), consciousness (*saṃvit*), understanding (*dhiṣaṇā*), thought (*dhī*), mental faculty (*manīṣā*), discernment (*śemuṣī*), retentive power (*medhā*), and intelligence (*buddhi*)—these and similar terms are synonyms for knowledge. Intellect itself, through the distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), takes the form of pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort. There is no evidence for the existence of knowledge as something distinct from that which is accepted as the cause of pleasure and so forth; for the conventional usage of "I desire" or "I hate" is accounted for by a particular kind of knowledge, just like the usage of "I remember" and the like.

If it is objected: "But has it not been stated that desire, resolve, doubt, faith, lack of faith, steadfastness, lack of steadfastness, shame, intelligence, and fear—all this is merely the mind? How then can it be of the nature of knowledge? We reply: No; since it is a rule that knowledge necessarily requires the mind as its auxiliary cause, the statement "it is merely the mind" was made figuratively, and thus there is no contradiction.

Thus, there are perception, inference, scripture, memory, doubt, certainty, error, delusion, discrimination, resolve, infatuation, attachment, aversion, intoxication, envy, fortitude, fickleness, hypocrisy, greed, anger, pride, arrogance, hostility, dogmatic adherence, despondency, bliss, and so forth; as well as intelligence, dullness, trust, contentment, nourishment, elevation, fatigue, fame, detachment, passion, friendliness, compassion, the desire for liberation, modesty, endurance, inquiry, the desire to conquer, joy, forgiveness, the desire to act, loathing, cultivation of thought, deceit, and malice.

Desire to kill, thirst, evil longing, latent impressions, evil impressions, deliberation, devotion, surrender, and so forth—these infinite qualities of the individual soul (*jīvātman*) are indeed particular states of the attribute that constitutes knowledge (*dharmabhūtajñāna*). Likewise, the Lord’s infinite auspicious qualities—such as knowledge, power, strength, sovereignty, valor, splendor, good character, affection, gentleness, straightforwardness, friendliness, equanimity, compassion, sweetness, profundity, magnanimity, cleverness, steadfastness, heroism, and prowess—are expansions of His knowledge and power.
This is the definition of the nature of the Lord’s auspicious qualities.

In this context, "knowledge" (jñāna) consists of direct realization of all things. "Power" (śakti) is the capacity to accomplish the impossible. "Strength" (bala) is the capacity for maintenance. "Sovereignty" (aiśvarya) is the capacity for governance. "Vigor" (vīrya) is the state of being unchangeable. "Splendor" (tejas) is the capacity to overcome others. "Gentleness" (sauśīlya) is the close and inseparable union of the great with the humble. "Affection" (vātsalya) is the perception of merit even in a fault, or the failure to perceive faults at all. "Tenderness" (mārdava) is the inability to endure the separation of those who have sought refuge. "Uprightness" (ārjava) is the uniformity of mind, speech, and body.

Friendliness (*sauhārda*) is the state of being intent on protecting others without regard for one's own existence. Equanimity (*sāmya*) is the state of being a refuge for all without regard for lineage, conduct, virtues, or other such qualities. Compassion (*kāruṇya*) is the desire to dispel the suffering of others without regard for one's own interest (*svaprayojana*), or it is the inability to endure the suffering of others (*paraduḥkhāsahiṣṇutva*). Sweetness (*mādhurya*) is the state of being delicious even when serving as a means (*upāya*), like milk. Profundity (*gāmbhīrya*) is the state of being utterly unfathomable from the very root, due to qualities such as being munificent toward those who are devoted.

Generosity (*audārya*) is the lack of satiety even after giving immeasurable (*aparimita*) or abundant (*prabhūta*) gifts. Skillfulness (*cāturya*) is the concealment of the faults of those who have sought refuge. Steadfastness (*sthairya*) is the state of being unshakable. Fortitude (*dhairya*) is the state of having an unbroken vow. Heroism (*śaurya*) is the capacity to penetrate the forces of the enemy. Valor (*parākrama*) is the repelling of those [forces]. Other such qualities are to be inferred accordingly.

The nature of devotion (*bhakti*) and surrender (*prapatti*), which are specific forms of knowledge, is briefly stated here. It is the Lord alone who, being pleased by means of devotion and surrender, grants liberation; therefore, these two constitute the means to liberation. [Regarding those] such as *karmayoga* and *jñānayoga*, which are described as means to liberation as being inseparable from devotion, their status as instruments of attainment is mediated solely through devotion (their status as means being intended for specific individuals).
[Now follows] the definition of the nature of *karmayoga*.

What is called *karmayoga* is a specific type of action undertaken—according to one's capacity and based on the knowledge of the true nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*) through instruction—which is free from attachment to results and consists of prohibited, optional, obligatory, and occasional duties. It is divided into various forms such as the worship of deities, austerity, pilgrimage, giving, sacrifice, and so forth. This [type of karma], by removing the impurities residing in the individual soul, gives rise to the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*), and thereby (or directly) becomes the producer of the yoga of knowledge; this is the definition of its essential nature.

The yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*) is a specific form of contemplation upon one's own self as distinct from *prakṛti* and subservient to the Lord, for one whose internal organ has been purified by the yoga of action (*karmayoga*). Its application is directly toward devotion (*bhakti*). In this manner, the independence and the applicability to devotion of other means of realization should also be inferred according to the authoritative scriptures. This concludes the definition of the nature of the yoga of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*).

That which is called *bhaktiyoga* consists of the eight limbs—*yama*, *niyama*, *āsana*, *prāṇāyāma*, *pratyāhāra*, *dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi*—and takes the form of an uninterrupted continuity of mindfulness, like a stream of oil. It is produced by a sevenfold set of means consisting of discrimination (*viveka*), detachment (*vimoka*), practice (*abhyāsa*), action (*kriyā*), auspiciousness (*kalyāṇa*), non-dejection (*anavasāda*), and non-exultation (*anudgharṣa*). Among these, "discrimination" (*viveka*) is the purification of the body from food that is tainted by its species, source, or occasion. "Detachment" (*vimoka*) is the absence of attachment to desires. "Practice" (*abhyāsa*) is the repeated cultivation of the object of focus.

Action consists of the performance of the five great sacrifices and other rites according to one's capacity; auspicious qualities include truthfulness, straightforwardness, compassion, generosity, non-violence, and so forth; and lack of despondency refers to the absence of dejection.

Lack of exultation (*anuddharṣa*) means the absence of contentment; it signifies that excessive satisfaction is also an obstacle. Thus, devotion (*bhakti*), when sustained by the sevenfold means, becomes identical in form to direct perception (*darśana*) and culminates in the final realization (*antima-pratyaya*). This final realization occurs either at the end of this present body or at the end of another body. And this devotion—denoted by such terms as "knowing" (*vedana*), "meditation" (*dhyāna*), and "worship" (*upāsana*)—proceeds through the stages of supreme devotion (*parabhakti*), supreme knowledge (*parajñāna*), and ultimate devotion (*paramabhakti*), and has surrender (*prapatti*) as its constituent limb.

It is of two kinds, distinguished as *sādhanabhakti* (devotion as means) and *phalabhakti* (devotion as fruit). *Sādhanabhakti* is that which is produced by the aforementioned means. *Phalabhakti*, however, is produced by the grace of the Lord and resides in those such as Śrī Parāṅkuśanātha and others. The use of the word "devotion" (*bhakti*) in passages such as "affection for my devotees" and in reference to praise, prostration, and so forth, is figurative. In the Vedāntas, it is established that meditation alone is what is enjoined.

If it be objected: "Since hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*) are also enjoined in the Vedāntas, how can it be said that meditation (*dhyāna*) alone is enjoined?"—it is replied as follows: A person who has studied the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga-veda*), seeing that the comprehension of the purposeful meaning [of the scriptures] does not arise [automatically], engages in hearing by himself for the sake of determining that meaning. Thus, because hearing is already established, it is merely restated (*anuvāda*). Reflection is also restated because its purpose is to stabilize what was heard. Therefore, since it is meditation alone that is enjoined, there is no contradiction.
Furthermore, due to the distinction between types of knowledge (*vidyā-bheda*), there is a distinction between types of devotion (*bhakti-bheda*).

Devotion, which is expressed by the term *dhyāna*, becomes manifold according to the different types of knowledge (*vidyā*). That knowledge is of two kinds: that which has worldly fruits and that which has liberation as its fruit. Among these, those with worldly fruits include the *udgītha-vidyā* and others. Those with liberation as their fruit, however, are the various forms of Brahman-knowledge (*brahma-vidyā*), such as the *antarikṣa-vidyā*, *antarāditya-vidyā*, *dahara-vidyā*, *bhūma-vidyā*, *sad-vidyā*, *madhu-vidyā*, *upakosala-vidyā*, *śāṇḍilya-vidyā*, *puruṣa-vidyā*, *pratardana-vidyā*, *vaiśvānara-vidyā*, *pañcāgni-vidyā*, and so forth.
[Now follows] the description of the *nyāsa-vidyā*.

The science of *nyāsa* is *prapatti*. It is defined as the prayer for Him alone as the sole means, preceded by great confidence, regarding one's desired goal which cannot be accomplished by any other means; it is called *prapatti* or *śaraṇāgati*. It is endowed with five limbs: the resolve to act favorably, the avoidance of what is unfavorable, the conviction that He will protect, the choice of Him as the protector, and the surrender of oneself along with the sense of helplessness. This bestows liberation at the end of this body.

The renunciation (*nyāsa*)—which is independent of the final cognition, to be performed all at once, denoted by such terms as "taking refuge" (*śaraṇāgati*), and consisting of a specific form of knowledge—must be understood from the mouth of a Guru according to the secret scriptures and the authentic tradition. Since this [work] was composed for the purpose of instructing beginners, it is not revealed here; thus, I shall desist.
[This concludes] the refutations of other doctrines concerning the means to liberation.

The refutation of the means taught by others follows from the acceptance of devotion (*bhakti*) and surrender (*prapatti*) alone as the instruments for liberation. For instance, among those outside the Vedic fold, in the view of some, since a self distinct from the body is not admitted, the very engagement toward liberation is impossible. In the view of others, because cognition is momentary and that [cognition] itself is the self, whose engagement would there be? If it is argued that it belongs to the "stream" (*santāna*), no; for one person should not exert effort for the sake of another, and thus there can be no engagement.

In the opinion of others, there is no engagement [with spiritual practice] because of the doctrine of manifoldness (*anekāntavāda*), according to which [dharma and adharma], sentient and insentient beings, and so forth, follow the method of the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī*). In the systems of the Vaiśeṣikas and others, engagement by anyone is impossible, as liberation is like that of a stone. In the systems of the Sāṅkhyas and others, because God is not accepted, there is no engagement due to doubt as to whether liberation belongs to the *puruṣa* or to *prakṛti*. In the Māyā-vāda system, there is no engagement because a conventional statement does not produce knowledge of ultimate non-difference.

The doctrine of the combination (*samuccaya*) of ritual action and knowledge propounded by Bhāskara and Yādava is also refuted by the aforementioned reasoning. As for the Śaiva system, it is rejected because it accepts Paśupati as the goal to be attained and because it accepts practices such as the smearing of ashes—which are contrary to the Vedas—as means to that end. Thus has *mati* been defined.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Definition of *Buddhi* (Attribute-Consciousness)," in the *Śārīrakaparibhāṣā*, a commentary on the *Yatīndramatadīpikā*, composed by Śrīnivāsadāsa, the first disciple of the venerable Mahācārya, the ornament of the Vādhūla lineage.
Now begins the eighth chapter.

Now the individual soul (*jīva*) is defined. Self-consciousness (*pratyaktva*), consciousness (*cetanatva*), selfhood (*ātmatva*), agency (*kartṛtva*), and so forth, are characteristics common to both the Lord (*īśvara*) and the individual soul. Self-consciousness means being manifest to oneself by oneself alone. Consciousness means being the substratum of knowledge. Selfhood means being related to a body. Agency means being the substratum of volition and cognition.

Thus, the specific characteristics of the individual soul (jīva), which has been defined by its general characteristic, are now stated: it is consciousness while being atomic in size; it is consciousness while being inherently subordinate [to the Self]. In this manner, its qualities such as being supported, being subject to command, having agency dependent on another, and being dependent on others are to be inferred. This constitutes the proof of the soul's distinctness from the body, the senses, and so forth.

And that [Self] is distinct from the body, the senses, the mind, the vital breaths, and the intellect. It is distinguished from the body by the cognition "this is my body. Likewise, it is distinguished from the external senses by such cognitions as "I see with the eye," "I hear with the sense of hearing," and "I speak with speech. It is distinguished from the mind, the vital breaths, and the intellect by the cognition "I know through the mind"—since the mind is perceived as the instrument of knowledge—and by the expression of distinction "my vital breaths" and the cognition "I am the knower.
[The following is the demonstration of the atomic dimension of the Self.]

And that [self] is of atomic dimension (*aṇu-parimāṇa*), because of scriptural statements regarding its passing out [of the body] and so forth, and in accordance with the evidence. One should not raise the objection: "If it is atomic, how can there be the simultaneous experience of multiple objects? For this is possible through the pervasion of the knowledge that has become an attribute (*dharma-bhūta-jñāna*). By this very principle, the simultaneous assumption of multiple bodies by those such as Saubhari and by liberated souls (*mukta*) is also rendered possible.

And it is eternal, because of the recognition of objects previously experienced. If it is asked, "If the soul (*jīva*) is eternal, how can there be the cognition that 'the soul is born' or 'the soul is destroyed'?", we reply: no, for it is established that the soul's connection with a body is its birth, and its separation from that [body] is its destruction; the essential nature of the soul is indeed eternal.

And that [Self] is distinct in each body. Just as there is the cognition "one jar" with respect to all jars of the same dimension, and just as there is the cognition "one grain of rice" in a heap of rice, so too is there the conventional usage of "oneness" due to the uniformity of the form of consciousness; however, this is not oneness of essential nature (*svarūpa*), because that would contradict the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). By its own nature, it is blissful, but through the influence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), it undergoes transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). Furthermore, it is the agent, the enjoyer, and possesses a body. With respect to *prakṛti*, it is the embodied one (*śarīrin*); with respect to the Lord (*īśvara*), it is the body.

Its self-luminosity is established by both direct perception and scripture. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: the Self is self-luminous because it is consciousness (*jñāna*), just like the attribute-consciousness (*dharmabhūtajñāna*). Consciousness, atomicity, purity, and so forth are the attributes that define its essential nature (*svarūpa*). This concludes the refutation of other views regarding the Self.

By this [the following views are refuted]: the Buddhist position that the self is a momentary continuum because cognition is momentary; the Cārvāka position that the self is limited by the body because the body consists of the four elements; the Jaina position that the self is of the same dimension as the body—thus being the size of an elephant in an elephant’s body and the size of an ant in an ant’s body; the Sāṅkhya position that agency, enjoyership, and so forth belong to *prakṛti* alone and not to the *puruṣa*; and the Yādava position that the individual soul (*jīva*) is a portion of Brahman.

The following contradictory positions have been refuted: Bhāskara’s view that the individual soul (*jīva*) is a portion of Brahman delimited by adjuncts (*upādhi*); the theory of a single soul imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*); and the theory of multiple souls delimited by internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*), among others; as well as the theory of the soul's omnipresence (*vibhutva*).

If it is objected: "But if the all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) is not accepted, how can there be the experience of results in another location produced by unseen merit or demerit (*adṛṣṭa*)?", we reply: No, for even in the absence of a [physical] connection, it is possible through the power of *adṛṣṭa*. What is called *adṛṣṭa* is a specific cognition produced by a particular action performed by the individual soul that generates the Lord's pleasure. That specific [cognition], which is indeed the Lord's own volition (*saṅkalpa*), resides in the Lord who is all-pervasive in nature. Therefore, there is no contradiction regarding the attainment of the result. As for the classification of the individual soul, that soul is threefold, distinguished as bound (*baddha*), liberated (*mukta*), and eternal (*nitya*).

Among them, those called "bound" (baddha) are the specific sentient beings, from Brahmā down to insects, who follow the cycle of transmigration and inhabit the shell of the cosmic egg consisting of fourteen worlds. From the navel-lotus of the illustrious Nārāyaṇa was born Brahmā; from Brahmā, Rudra; and again from Brahmā arose the yogis such as Sanaka, the divine sages (devarṣi) such as Nārada, the brahmin-sages (brahmarṣi) such as Vasiṣṭha, and the nine Prajāpatis such as Pulastya, Marīci, Dakṣa, and Kaśyapa.

From them [proceed] the gods, the guardians of the directions, the fourteen Indras, the fourteen Manus, the Asuras, the Pitṛs, the Siddhas, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Kiṃpurushas, Vidyādharas, and so forth; the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, the two Aśvins, and the Dānavas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Piśācas, Guhyakas, and others. Thus, the divine lineages are of many kinds. Humans also are of many kinds, distinguished by the divisions of castes such as Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, Śūdra, and so on. Animals also are of many kinds, distinguished by the divisions of domestic animals, wild beasts, birds, reptiles, insects, worms, and so forth.

Immobile beings (*sthāvara*) are also of many kinds, distinguished as trees, shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, grasses, and so forth. Trees and the like indeed possess a connection with some degree of knowledge directed toward functions such as drawing up water; for it has been stated that this [knowledge] is merely slight in those lacking vital breath (*aprāṇavat*). Therefore, bound souls (*baddha*) are divided into the categories of gods, humans, animals, and immobile beings. Furthermore, these consist of the womb-born (*jarāyuja*), egg-born (*aṇḍaja*), soil-born (*udbhija*), and sweat-born (*svedaja*). Gods and humans are womb-born.

Among them, Brahmā, Rudra, and others; Sanaka and others; Sītā, Draupadī, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, and others; as well as spirits, *vetālas*, and so forth, are born without a womb (*ayonija*). Animals and the like are born from the womb (*jarāyuja*), from eggs (*aṇḍaja*), or from sweat (*svedaja*). Plants and the like are born from sprouts (*udbhijja*).

Bound in this manner by the logic of the seed and the sprout, they have proceeded through the flow of time since beginningless ages due to the uneven current of ignorance (*avidyā*), karma, latent impressions (*vāsanā*), inclination (*ruci*), and connection with primordial nature (*prakṛti*). Revolving like a wheel, they possess various and manifold experiences such as conception, birth, infancy, youth, waking, dreaming, deep sleep, fainting, old age, death, and the going to heaven or hell. They are tormented by the three unbearable types of suffering (*tāpa*) in their endless and beginningless modes, and they suffer the interruption of the experience of the Blessed Lord which was spontaneously attained [by them]. This is the classification of living beings who are subject to the scriptures.

They are of two kinds: those subject to the scriptures (*śāstravaśya*) and those not subject to them (*tadavaśya*). Among these, those who are bound (*baddha*) and whose knowledge is dependent upon the instruments of perception possess subjection to the scriptures. This does not apply to animals, stationary beings (*sthāvara*), and so forth. Those subject to the scriptures are of two types: those desiring enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*) and those desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*). Among them, those desiring enjoyment are devoted to the three aims of human life (*traivargika-puruṣārtha*). They are further divided into two: those intent on wealth and pleasure (*artha-kāma*) and those intent on dharma. Those solely intent on wealth and pleasure are characterized by the conceit that the body is the self (*dehātmābhimānin*).

And those devoted to *dharma* are those who are intent upon sacrifice, charity, austerity, pilgrimage to sacred sites, and so forth—characterized by the definition of *dharma* as "that which is beneficial and defined by Vedic injunction" (*codanālakṣaṇo 'rtho dharmaḥ*), which is the means for attaining supermundane welfare (*alaukika-śreyaḥ*). They possess the conceit of a self distinct from the body and know that there is a world beyond. Those devoted to *dharma* are of two kinds: those devoted to other deities and those devoted to the Blessed Lord.

Those devoted to other deities are those intent on the propitiation of Brahmā, Rudra, Agni, Indra, and so forth. Those devoted to the Blessed Lord (*bhagavat*), however, are the qualified aspirants described as "the afflicted," "the seeker of knowledge," and "the seeker of wealth. The afflicted is one who desires the recovery of lost sovereignty. The seeker of wealth is one who desires unprecedented sovereignty. Seekers of liberation (*mumukṣu*) are of two kinds: those intent on *kaivalya* and those intent on *mokṣa*. *Kaivalya* is the experience of one's own self as dissociated from primordial nature (*prakṛti*) through the yoga of knowledge.

Some say that this experience is the experience of one's own self distinct from the experience of the Lord, occurring in some corner for one who has reached the supreme state via the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*), according to the analogy of a wife who leaves her husband. Others say that because of the scriptural teaching of non-return for one who has gone by the path of light, this experience of one's own self occurs in some region within the sphere of *prakṛti* itself.
These are the distinctions among those seeking liberation who are intent on final release.

Those intent on liberation (*mokṣaparāḥ*) are of two kinds: the devotees (*bhaktāḥ*) and the surrendered ones (*prapannāḥ*). As for the devotees, they are those who have studied the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga*) and the Upanishads (*saśiraska*), and through their familiarity with the Purva and Uttara Mīmāṃsā, have ascertained Brahman—which is distinct from the conscious and the unconscious, consists of unsurpassed and infinite bliss, is the antithesis of all that is to be rejected, and is composed of all auspicious attributes—and having adopted devotion (*bhakti*) along with its limbs as the means for attaining That, they desire to attain liberation through it. Eligibility for devotion belongs only to the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*); however, it also exists for the gods and others.

Because both the desire for the goal (*arthitva*) and the capacity (*sāmarthya*) are present [in Śūdras], they do not have the qualification [for Vedic study]; this is because it would contradict the *apaśūdrādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning those other than Śūdras). However, the nature of devotion (*bhakti*) has been established in the *Buddhipariccheda*. Devotees are of two kinds: those established in *sādhana-bhakti* (devotion as means), such as Vyāsa and others; and those established in *sādhya-bhakti* (devotion as the end to be attained). Those established in *sādhana-bhakti* are Vyāsa and others; those established in *sādhya-bhakti* are Nātha and others.

Distinguished by the quality of having nothing else as his sole resort, he has taken refuge in and surrendered to the Blessed One. He is of two kinds: one intent on the three aims of life (*traivargika*) and one intent on liberation (*mokṣa*). The one intent on the three aims is one who desires the dharma, wealth, and pleasure from the Blessed One alone.

One who is intent on liberation, through association with the virtuous, attains discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal supreme Reality. Upon the arising of world-weariness and the birth of a desire for liberation due to that dispassion, he approaches a Guru characterized by the marks of a teacher—such as being perfected in the Vedas—for the sake of achieving that goal. Through him, he takes refuge in Śrī, who is the means of human effort (*puruṣakāra*). Being incapable of other means such as devotion and so forth, and therefore destitute and having no other recourse, he accepts the feet of the glorious Nārāyaṇa alone as his means; he is the one who has taken refuge (*prapanna*).

Surrender (*prapatti*) is open to all who are eligible. One who has surrendered is of two kinds: the *ekāntin* and the *paramaikāntin*. He who desires from the Lord alone even other fruits along with the fruit of liberation is an *ekāntin*; the meaning is that he is devoid of any other deity. He who does not desire any fruit other than devotion and knowledge, even from the Lord, is a *paramaikāntin*. He is further divided into two types based on the distinction between the arrogant (*dṛpta*) and the distressed (*ārta*).

Thinking "this must necessarily be experienced," he experiences the *prārabdha* karma while awaiting the time of the end of this body; yet, longing for liberation, he is filled with pride—pride born from the unbearable nature of worldly existence, which is like standing in the midst of a fiercely blazing fire—and thus, desiring liberation, he becomes distressed at the very moment following his surrender (*prapatti*).

One who is called "liberated" (mukta) is one who, immediately after embracing the means (upāya), performs actions consisting of service (kaiṅkarya) to the Lord—both obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika)—as their own primary purpose; who avoids [attachment to] the Lord, His devotees, and the teachers; and who, at the time of death, consigns both good and evil deeds, as well as friends and enemies, into the Supreme Self within the heart by means of speech, mind, and so forth. Having thus come to rest in the Supreme Self within the heart, he enters the *suṣumnā* channel which serves as the gateway to liberation, exits through the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmāraṇḍhra*) by that path, and [unites] with the one within the heart.

Having gone to the world of fire (*agniloka*) by way of the sun’s rays, he is honored on the path by the presiding deities of the day, the bright fortnight, the northern solstice, the year, and so forth, as well as by Vāyu; then, piercing the solar orb through the aperture of the sky (*nabhorandhra*)—the opening of the chariot wheel—he enters the world of the sun. Thereafter, accompanied by the escorting hosts (*ātivāhika-gaṇa*) of the Moon, Lightning, Varuṇa, Indra, and Prajāpati, who show him the way, he passes through those respective worlds with due hospitality, and finally crosses the Virajā river, which marks the boundary of the limit of Prakṛti-Vaiṣṇava-vaikuṇṭha.

Leaving behind the subtle body, by the touch of the hand of an amānava, he becomes endowed with a non-material, divine (auspicious) form, four-armed and adorned with the ornaments of Brahmā; having entered the divine city named Śrī Vaikuṇṭha with the permission of the gatekeepers of the city known as Indra and Prajāpati, and having passed beyond the gateway with its long ramparts adorned with banners, he beholds the lake of nectar called Airammada and the Aśvattha tree named Somasavana.

Attended by five hundred divine apsarases such as those mentioned beginning with "A hundred with garlands in hand," adorned with the fragrance of Brahman and other qualities, and having bowed to the local deities such as Ānanda, Garuḍa, and Viṣvaksena, he was highly honored by them. Having reached the great jeweled pavilion and bowed to his own teachers near the couch, he approached the couch; there, upon the lotus on the seat of Dharmādhipī, he beheld [the Lord] together with Śrī, Bhūmi, and Nīlā, being served by Ananta and Vimala and others holding chowries in their hands.

Having beheld the Blessed One—who was endowed with divine weapons such as the conch and the discus; who was blazing with a crown, tiara, crest-jewel, and makara-earrings; and who was adorned with immeasurable divine ornaments such as necklaces, strings of pearls, armlets, bracelets, the *śrīvatsa* mark, the *kaustubha* gem, a pearl girdle for the belly, yellow garments, a waist-belt, and anklets—and who was an ocean of immeasurable, noble, and auspicious qualities; he bowed his head at the pair of the Lord’s lotus feet, ascended the couch by foot, and being placed upon the Lord’s own lap, was asked, "Who are you?"

Having declared, "I am of the nature of Brahman" (or "I am the retinue of Brahman," or "I am the radiance of Brahman"), and being gladdened by that [realization], one who—due to the excellence of intense joy born from that experience—finds singular delight in every form of service appropriate for all places, all times, and all conditions; who has manifested the eight divine qualities (*guṇāṣṭaka*) and possesses the experience of Brahman without any upper limit—he is called "liberated. The scriptural statement regarding the liberated soul's attainment of equality with Brahman refers only to equality in enjoyment, because it is established that [the soul] is excluded from the activity of governing the world.
For such a one, multiplicity and wandering through all the worlds are possible.

One should not raise the objection: "Since it is taught that the liberated one does not return, how can there be movement in this world? For the prohibition applies only to that which is produced by karma; movement by one's own will is therefore logical. Thus, the liberated one, dependent upon the will of the Lord, moves everywhere according to his own desire.

The *nityas* (eternal beings) are those such as Ananta, Garuḍa, Viṣvaksena, and others, who—by never at any time performing any action contrary to the will of the Lord—are free from the possibility of the contraction of knowledge (*jñānasaṅkoca*). Their incarnations (*avatāras*), however, occur solely by their own will, just like the incarnations of the Lord. Thus has the individual soul (*jīva*) been described, distinguished by the divisions of the bound (*baddha*), the liberated (*mukta*), and the eternal (*nitya*).

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Individual Soul," in the *Yatīndramatadīpikā*, a treatise on the technical terminology of the Śārīraka [Vedānta], composed by Śrīnivāsadāsa, the first disciple of the venerable Mahācārya, the ornament of the Vādhūla lineage.
Now begins the ninth chapter.

Next, the Lord (Īśvara) is defined. The characteristics of the Lord include: being the sovereign of all, being the ultimate substratum of all, being the one to be propitiated by all rites, being the bestower of the fruits of all actions, being the support of all, being the producer of all effects, (being denotable by all words), and having all substances—both Himself and others—as His body.
This concludes the establishment of the Lord as the cause of the universe.

This Lord, in His aspect as qualified by subtle consciousness and matter (*cid-acit*), is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of the universe; in His aspect as qualified by volition (*saṅkalpa*), He is the instrumental cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*); and in His aspect as the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) of time and other factors, He is the auxiliary cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*). A substance capable of modification into the form of an effect is the material cause. That which brings about the transformation into the state of an effect is the instrumental cause. An entity that serves as an instrument for the production of the effect is the auxiliary cause.

Alternatively, with respect to a specific nature characterized by successive states, that which is characterized by a specific preceding state invariably occurring in accordance with it is the material cause (*upādāna*). For example, with respect to the substance characterized by the state of being a jar, that very same substance characterized by the state of being a lump [of clay] is the material cause. A cause required in a form distinct from the orientation toward transformation (*pariṇāmaunmukhya*) is the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). On this view, the auxiliary cause (*sahakārikāraṇa*) is subsumed within the instrumental cause.

Thus, whether on the view of three causes or the view of two causes, because he is characterized by the defining marks of causality, the status of being the cause of the entire universe belongs to the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa alone.
This is the demonstration that the causality of the universe culminates in Nārāyaṇa.

Now, if it is asked, "How is the final conclusion regarding Nārāyaṇa’s status as the cause established? it is said in reply: It is established precisely through an inquiry into the Vedāntic texts aided by reasoning (*nyāya*). For instance: First of all, it is not tenable that *prakṛti* is the cause of the world, because it lacks the quality of being a "seer" (*īkṣitṛtva*) and so forth. In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, the status of being the cause of the world is perceived for those things denoted by the words "Sat" and "Prāṇa. In the Vājasaneyaka [Bṛhadāraṇyaka], the status of being the cause of the world is perceived for that which is denoted by the word "Brahman."

When it must be established that the causal statements have a single referent according to the principle of "all branches being authoritative" (*sarva-śākhā-pratyaya-nyāya*), one must state that words denoting a general [entity], such as "Being" (*sat*) and so forth, culminate in the specific entity that is Brahman, according to the principle of the "goat and the animal" (*chāga-paśu-nyāya*).

Thus, when by the aforementioned principle the word "Brahman" culminates in that which is denoted by the word "Self" (*ātman*) as stated in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad, there arises the inquiry: "What is that which is denoted by the word 'Self'? Is it Indra, well-known from the Śruti; or Agni, likewise well-known; or Sūrya, well-known as an object of meditation; or Soma, mentioned as the cause?

When Kubera, Yama, or Varuṇa are mentioned as the bestower of desired objects, there arises a doubt; however, because it is heard in scripture that these deities are subject to karma, possess limited sovereignty, and are themselves subject to dissolution, they are not the cause of the universe. Rather, in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, the causality of Śiva is revealed. Likewise, in the Atharvaśikhā, the state of being the object of meditation for the one denoted by the word "Śambhu" is revealed. Similarly, in the Atharvaśiras, the identity with all things (sarvātmakatva) of the one denoted by the word "Rudra" is declared.

In the Taittirīya [Upaniṣad], Hiraṇyagarbha is perceived as the cause of the world. Here too, by the principle of the general and the particular, it is appropriate that the words Śiva, Śambhu, and Rudra terminate in the specific referent denoted by the term Hiraṇyagarbha.

The word *śiva* possesses the quality of denoting auspiciousness through such expressions as "May there be welfare for all the worlds," "May the ritual action be auspicious," and "May your paths be auspicious. The word *rudra*, however, denotes fire. Likewise, common terms such as *maheśvara* and *śambhu* also ultimately refer to the Four-faced One (Brahmā) by virtue of their etymological components. It should not be suspected that words like *śiva*, which denote the Cause, might—by their primary function (*mukhyavṛtti*)—refer instead to Rudra.

Since it is heard that Rudra was born from the four-faced one (Brahmā), and because he is heard to be "one whose evil has not been destroyed," Rudra cannot be the ultimate cause. Therefore, words such as Śiva ultimately refer to the four-faced one, who is denoted by terms like Hiraṇyagarbha, Prajāpati, and Svayambhū.

Thus, because the *Mahopaniṣad*, *Nārāyaṇopaniṣad*, *Subālopaniṣad*, the *Maitrāyaṇīya-puruṣasūkta*, the *Nārāyaṇānuvāka*, the *Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa*, and other such texts establish that Nārāyaṇa alone is the supreme cause, is denotable by all words, is the bestower of liberation, and possesses the body of the entire universe, it is logical that the terms *Svayambhū*, *Hiraṇyagarbha*, and *Prajāpati* terminate in Nārāyaṇa; therefore, Nārāyaṇa alone is the cause of the entire world and the object to be known through all the Vedas.

Now, one should not entertain the doubt that the Antarāditya-vidyā is devoted to Rudra; for its devotion to Viṣṇu alone is established by many authorities. Furthermore, [the objection that it refers to Rudra] is refuted because the word *bharga* is demonstrated to end in *s*, as in the form ‘*harassmaraharobharga*’ where *rudra* ends in *a*. If so, one should not suspect that the Dahara-vidyā is devoted to Rudra, since Rudra is presented therein as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of Nārāyaṇa, who is denoted by the word *ākāśa*.

Because it is stated therein that the collection of qualities residing within Nārāyaṇa alone is the object of meditation; this same principle should be applied to all other Vidyās as well. Therefore, the Supreme Brahman, Nārāyaṇa alone—who consists of all auspicious qualities, who is distinct from both Prakṛti and Puruṣa, and who is qualified by them—is the cause of the world.

Now, an objection may be raised: According to the Śrutis on non-duality (advaita), Brahman alone is real and devoid of qualities (nirguṇa). Everything else—the knower, the known, and so forth—is superimposed upon that very [Brahman] and is entirely illusory (mithyā). Brahman undergoes transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) through ignorance (avidyā), and the knowledge of non-difference expressed in passages such as "That thou art" (tattvamasi) is what removes that [ignorance].

If it is argued that, since those belonging to other schools establish that the purport of the Vedāntas is Brahman as the undifferentiated pure consciousness (*nirviśeṣacinmātra*), how can the purport be Nārāyaṇa, and why is there a description of Him as being composed of all auspicious qualities (*kalyāṇaguṇa*) and so forth? To this, it is replied:

Once Nārāyaṇa’s status as the cause has been established by the scriptural passages demonstrating causality, and once the contradiction between the Śrutis concerning difference and non-difference has been resolved through the mediation of Śrutis that reconcile them by way of different subject matters; and since the Śrutis teaching the Nirguṇa Brahman negate only those qualities that are to be abandoned; and since the ignorance (*avidyā*) which fashions the knower, the known, and so forth, is itself devoid of any basis in valid authority; and since the effects of Brahman are real; and since, through ignorance in the context of *saṃsāra*, the defects residing in the individual soul (*jīva*) may also pertain to Brahman; and because it is impossible to state any other means for their removal—[it follows that Brahman is both the material and efficient cause].

Therefore, since the doctrine of non-duality (advaitavāda) is untenable, there is no establishment of Brahman as mere consciousness devoid of attributes. Consequently, it is only Nārāyaṇa who can possess the connection with qualities such as being the cause of the universe and the bestower of liberation; thus, Brahman is indeed possessed of attributes. The tradition of the Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedāntins is that Brahman qualified by subtle consciousness and matter is the cause, while Brahman qualified by gross consciousness and matter is the effect; thus, the effect is non-different from the cause.

Thus, by accepting [the existence of] Īśvara, the doctrines of the Sāṃkhya and Mīmāṃsaka schools and others who deny His existence are refuted. By accepting His status as the material cause (*upādāna*), the doctrines of the Yoga, Pāśupata, and Naiyāyika schools are refuted, for they accept Īśvara merely as the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*). It is also logically consistent that Īśvara possesses, with respect to the effect, not only the nature of being both the material and efficient cause, but also agency (*kartṛtva*), instigation (*prerakatva*), control (*niyantṛtva*), governance (*praśāsitṛtva*), illumination (*kāśayitṛtva*), permission (*anumantṛtva*), cooperation (*sahakāritva*), and indifference (*udāsīnatva*).

Just as defects such as childhood, youth, and other stages belong to the body and not to the embodied soul (jīva), so too they belong to the Supreme Self who has both consciousness and unconsciousness as His body; thus there is no contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning His being changeless. Since the definition of a "body"—namely, being invariably supported by, subject to the will of, and subordinate to [another]—is found in the world, the Lord has the universe as His body and is untouched by the defects residing therein.

He is the Lord (Īśvara) and of the nature of all-pervasiveness (vibhu). All-pervasiveness means being omnipresent. That [pervasiveness] belongs to the Lord in three ways: by His essential nature (svarūpa), by His attribute of knowledge (dharmabhūtajñāna), and by His form (vigraha). He is called infinite (ananta). "Infinite" means devoid of the three kinds of limitation. The three kinds of limitation are: spatial, temporal, and substantial. Truthfulness, consciousness, bliss, purity, and so forth, are the attributes that define the essential nature of the Lord.

The powers of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) and so forth are attributes whose very nature is defined by Him. Omniscience (*sarvajñatva*), omnipotence (*sarvaśaktitva*), and so forth are attributes conducive to creation. Benevolence (*vātsalya*), gentleness (*sauśīlya*), amiability (*saumya*), and so forth are attributes conducive to taking refuge [in Him]. Compassion (*kārūṇya*) and so forth are attributes conducive to protection. The nature of these has been established in the section on the analysis of the intellect (*buddhi-pariccheda*); therefore, it is not elaborated upon here.

This Lord, after the creation of the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*), presides over the creation by dwelling as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) within Brahmā, Dakṣa, Kāla, and others. By assuming the forms of Viṣṇu’s incarnations and by acting as the inner controller of Manus, Kāla, and so forth, He becomes the protector. Furthermore, by being the inner controller of Rudra, Kāla, Antaka, and others, He effects dissolution. Thus, He is the agent of creation, preservation, and destruction.
In this manner, the Lord is fivefold, appearing in the forms of the Supreme (*para*), the Vyūha, the Vibhava, the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*), and the Archāvatāra.

Therein, "the other" refers to the glorious divine abode within the great jeweled pavilion in the city named Śrīmad-Vaikuṇṭha—which is protected by divine guardians of the city such as Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana, Śaṅkukarṇa, Sarvanetra, Sumukha, and Supratiṣṭhita, all equipped with divine weapons, ornaments, attendants, and retinues—and which is attended by gatekeepers such as Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, Bhadra, Subhadra, Jaya, Vijaya, Dhātṛ, and Vidhātṛ, within the three-quarters manifestation (*tripādvibhūti*).

Nārāyaṇa—designated by such terms as the Supreme Brahman and the Supreme Vāsudeva—is distinguished by a divine, auspicious form with four arms, seated upon a lion-throne fashioned from the eight qualities beginning with Dharma, reclining on the serpent Śeṣa, accompanied by Śrī, Bhū, Nīlā, and others, endowed with divine weapons such as the conch and discus, adorned with divine ornaments like the crown, and experienced by eternal attendants such as Ananta, Garuḍa, and Viṣvaksena, as well as other liberated souls intent on singing the Sāman hymns; he is characterized by an infinite multitude of auspicious attributes such as the power of knowledge.
This is the description of the Lord’s manifested form (vyūha-rūpa).

The one called Vyūha is indeed another [form] who, for the purpose of worship and for the purpose of the creation of the world and so forth, exists in fourfold division as Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha. Among these:

Vāsudeva is complete with the six attributes (*ṣāḍguṇya*). Saṅkarṣaṇa is characterized by knowledge (*jñāna*) and strength (*bala*); Pradyumna by sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) and heroism (*vīrya*); and Aniruddha by power (*śakti*) and splendor (*tejas*). This is the division of the attributes. Within these four, three each have descended as Keśava and the others, forming twelve further manifestations (*vyūha*), which are the presiding deities (*adhidaivata*) of the twelve months and the twelve Ādityas. Their placement upon the vertical marks (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) is prescribed; therein, Keśava has a golden luster and bears four discs.

Śyāma Nārāyaṇa is dark-complexioned and holds four conch shells; Mādhava has the luster of a jewel and possesses four maces. Govinda has the brilliance of the moon and holds four Śārṅga bows; Viṣṇu resembles the filaments of a lotus and possesses four plows. Madhusūdana has the luster of a lotus and holds four pestles; Trivikrama is the color of fire and possesses four swords. Vāmana has the brilliance of the rising sun and holds four thunderbolts; Śrīdhara has the luster of a white lotus and holds four spears. Hṛṣīkeśa has the radiance of lightning and holds four mallets.

Sūryābha (Sun-like) has a lotus-navel and bears five weapons; Indragopanibha (resembling the cochineal insect) is Dāmodara and holds four nooses. The description of the Lord’s *vibhava-rūpa* (manifestation of power): *vibhava* refers to the appearance in forms belonging to various specific classes. It is tenfold according to its primary renown, and these are the particular incarnations (*avatāra*) such as the Fish, the Tortoise, and others. Among them, the Matsya-avatāra (Fish incarnation) appeared for the purpose of restoring the authority of the Vedas to Brahmā after dispelling the Daityas who had stolen them. The Kūrma-avatāra (Tortoise incarnation) appeared as the support for Mount Mandara during the churning for the production of the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*), which serves as the cause for the gods’ freedom from old age and death.

The Varāha incarnation descended to lift up his own Earth, desiring to rescue people submerged in the ocean of *saṃsāra*. The Narasiṃha incarnation arose from the pillar in the house of the great demon for the sake of protecting those who have taken refuge in him. Having become Trivikrama, the Vāmana incarnation descended for the protection of the world by removing the sins of the universe with the water arising from his own lotus-feet. The Paraśurāma incarnation descended for the purpose of exterminating the wicked Kṣatriyas.

Śrī Rāma (Rāmacandra), the incarnation as Rāma, descended for the purpose of protecting those who have sought refuge and establishing the Dharma. Balabhadra, the incarnation as Balarāma, descended for the purpose of destroying Pralamba and others. Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the incarnation as Kṛṣṇa, descended for the purpose of bestowing the means to liberation. Kalki, the incarnation as Kalkin, descended for the purpose of expelling the unrighteous and promoting the complete Dharma (or for the purpose of releasing the world from the Kali age). Thus, within each of these ten incarnations, every single one manifests in infinite ways.

There are also thirty-six incarnations beginning with Padmanābha, as well as others such as Dadhibhakta, Hayagrīva, and Nara-Nārāyaṇa. Thus, these are of many kinds according to the sub-divisions known as primary (mukhya), secondary (gauṇa), complete (pūrṇa), partial (aṃśa), and those consisting of a descent of power (āveśa). Among them, the distinction between those who are to be worshipped and those who are not should be observed. The sole cause of the incarnations is the will [of the Lord], and not karma. Their purpose, however, is solely the protection of the virtuous preceded by the destruction of the wicked.

The nature of the Inner Controller (*antaryāmitva*) refers to the form of the Lord residing in the region of the heart, who is to be perceived by yogis as the friend of the individual soul (*jīvātman*) even during states of experiencing heaven, hell, and so forth. Although He exists together with the individual soul, He remains untouched by the defects inherent in that soul.
This is a description of the Lord in the form of an *arcāvatāra* (an incarnated image).

The *arcāvatāra* (incarnation in the form of an image) is a specific manifestation existing in houses, villages, cities, excellent regions, mountains, and so forth; it is free from the limitations of space and time, assumes as its body the materials and other objects favored by its devotees, and—being distinguished by a non-material (*aprākṛta*) body therein—remains dependent on the worshipper for bathing, eating, sitting, sleeping, and staying, while being all-enduring and complete. It is of four kinds, categorized as self-manifested (*svayaṃvyakta*), divine (*daiva*), perfected (*siddha*), and human (*mānuṣa*).

Thus, it is established by the authority of the Śruti and other means that even in these five states, the Blessed Lord exists as endowed with glory (śrī). By this, the doctrine of "formlessness" (niḥśrīkatva) mentioned in the Ākāśāgama is refuted. In this manner, the Lord has been defined.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Definition of the Lord," in the *Yatīndramatadīpikā*, a glossary of the Śārīraka [Sūtras], composed by Śrīnivāsadāsa, the first disciple of the venerable Mahācārya, the ornament of the Vādhūla lineage.
Now begins the tenth chapter.

Thus, following the determination of substances (*dravya*), the substance-less (*adravya*) is determined as it follows in the sequence. That which is devoid of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the substance-less. And that substance-less is of exactly ten kinds: *sattva*, *rajas*, *tamas*, sound, touch, form, taste, smell, conjunction, and power (*śakti*).

In that context, *sattva* is a non-substance (*adravya*) that is the cause of luminosity, pleasure, lightness, and so forth; it is supersensible and distinct from *śakti* and other such categories. It is of two kinds: pure *sattva* (*śuddhasattva*) and mixed *sattva* (*miśrasattva*). Pure *sattva* is the quality of *sattva* residing in a substance devoid of *rajas* and *tamas*; it exists in eternal glory (*nityavibhūti*) and, by figurative extension, in the Lord who impels it. Mixed *sattva* is the quality of *sattva* coexisting with *rajas* and *tamas*; it exists in the three qualities (*triguṇa*) and, by figurative extension, in the individual soul (*jīva*) who is connected to them.

Rajas is a non-substantial entity beyond the reach of the senses, distinct from power (*śakti*) and the like, which has its source in the activity of passion, thirst, greed, and so forth. Tamas is a non-substantial entity beyond the reach of the senses, distinct from power and the like, which has its cause in negligence, delusion, and so forth. All three of these pervade as far as primordial nature (*prakṛti*).

These [qualities] are common to all, being connected to the Puruṣa who is by nature subject [to them], impermanent, existing in an eternal continuum, equal during the state of dissolution (pralaya), and unequal at the beginning of creation; they are employed for the purposes of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal, and through the diversity of auxiliary factors such as the will of Īśvara, they cause mutual suppression and emergence. The quality of *sattva*, however, is the cause of happiness and the like consisting of right knowledge, and it bestows liberation (*mokṣa*). The quality of *rajas*, moreover, consists of passion and the like, is attached to action, is the cause of suffering and the like, and bestows the hereafter such as heaven.

The quality of *tamas*, however, is the cause of ignorance, indolence, and so forth, and it bestows the human state; therefore, the qualities such as *sattva* and the others are not of the nature of substances (*dravya*). Regarding the definition of sound (*śabda*):

sound is that which is perceivable by the ears of beings such as ourselves and exists within the five elements. It is of two kinds: consisting of phonemes (*varṇātmaka*) and non-phonemic (*avarṇātmaka*). That which consists of the fifty letters beginning with *a, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya,* and so on, is the phonemic type. Such sound is perceived by the sense organ of hearing. The perception of sound occurs either through the reaching of the auditory organ toward the sound or through the arrival of the manifesting air-currents.

If it is objected that sound (*śabda*) is perceived through scripture (*śruti*) to be a substance (*dravya*), and how then can it be non-substantial, we reply: its non-substantiality is established because its capacity to produce the *praṇava* (the sacred syllable *oṃ*) from the letter *a* and so forth occurs by way of its being expressed (*vācya*). The definition of touch (*sparśa*): Touch is a substance distinct from those things perceivable by the tactile organ of beings such as ourselves. It is of three kinds, distinguished as cold, hot, and neither-cold-nor-hot.

In water, there is a cold touch; in fire, a hot touch; and in earth and air, a touch that is neither hot nor cold. Furthermore, [touch] is of two kinds: produced by heating (*pākaja*) and not produced by heating (*apākaja*). The former exists in earth; the latter exists in the other three [elements]. Among these, specific touches such as those of nectar, poison, a balance stone, a cow, a Brahmin, and a Caṇḍāla are varieties produced by heating. [Now follows] the definition of color (*rūpa*).

Color (*rūpa*) is that which is perceptible solely by the visual faculty of ourselves and others, is distinct from heterogeneous substances, and is non-substantial (*adravya*). It is fourfold, distinguished as white, red, yellow, and black. Among these, the specific varieties of color belonging to water, silver, conch, mother-of-pearl, the moon, and so forth, are the sub-varieties of white. The specific varieties of color belonging to fire, the *japā* flower, the *dāḍima* fruit, the *bandhujīva* flower, coral, rubies, and so forth, are the sub-varieties of red. The specific varieties of color belonging to gold, orpiment, turmeric, and so forth, are the sub-varieties of yellow.

Specific varieties of black include emerald, the *madhukara* flower, clouds, darkness, the *tamāla* tree, *dūrvā* grass, and so forth. Some, following the authority of the scriptures (*śruti*), maintain that even yellowness is a sub-variety of red. Alternatively, color (*rūpa*) is of two kinds, distinguished as luminous (*bhāsvara*) and non-luminous (*abhāsvara*). That which belongs to fire is luminous; that which belongs to earth and water is non-luminous. Thus, there are only four types of color. By this, the view that there is a fifth color called "variegated" (*citra*) is refuted.
For this very reason, the existence of variegated taste, smell, and touch is also refuted.

Taste is that which is distinct from other things perceptible by the gustatory sense-organ of those such as ourselves. It is of six kinds, distinguished as sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent, and astringent. Among these, the tastes of sugarcane, milk, molasses, and so forth, are varieties of the sweet; the tastes of the mango, the tamarind, the *āmalaka* fruit, and so forth, are varieties of the sour; the tastes of rock salt, saline soil products, and so forth, are varieties of the salty; the tastes of the *kimpāka* fruit, the neem tree, and so forth, are varieties of the bitter; the tastes of ginger, black pepper, mustard seeds, and so forth, are varieties of the pungent; and the tastes of the *harītakī*, the *vibhītakī*, mango sprouts, and so forth, are varieties of the astringent.

Odor is that which is different from what is perceived by the olfactory organs of beings such as ourselves. It is of two kinds: fragrant (*surabhi*) and foul (*asurabhi*). Fragrances such as those of sandalwood, musk, saffron, and campaka are varieties of the fragrant; while putrid, cadaverous, and similar odors are varieties of the foul. This odor resides exclusively in earth and is differentiated by variations in its maturation (*pāka*). The perception of odor in air, water, and so forth is figurative (*aupacārikī*), resulting from contact with earthy substances, just as one says "the iron burns" [when it is red-hot].

Although all qualities exist in all elements through the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*), there is no contradiction, as this was stated with the intention of referring to predominance. The production of other qualities from cooking occurs in their own substratum; since the destruction of the substratum itself does not occur, the refutation of the *pīlu* (proponent of cooking) and other such views regarding cooking is established.
[Now follows] the definition of conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

Conjunction (*saṃyoga*) has the cause of the notion of being conjoined. It is a common quality (*sāmānyaguṇa*) residing in six substances. And its perceived co-location with its own absence does not entail contradiction, because it is conditioned by spatial parts (*aṃśa*). Furthermore, it is of two kinds based on the distinction between productive and non-productive [conjunction]: the former arises from the mutual impulsion of limited objects, such as that between two rams or two wrestlers; in some cases, it arises from the impulsion of only one, such as the conjunction between a post and a hawk.

Some also assert a "conjunction born of conjunction," such as the conjunction of the body with a book resulting from the conjunction of the hand with the book. That is not so, because it is accounted for by the conjunction of the hand with the book alone. By this, the "disjunction born of disjunction" is also refuted. Disjunction, too, is merely the absence of conjunction and is not a distinct quality. Furthermore, there is a conjunction of two all-pervading substances that is uncaused; such an uncaused conjunction of substances is accepted on the basis of scripture. The existence of an uncaused conjunction of substances is also established through inference.

Just as an all-pervading substance is established through its conjunction with another all-pervading substance; just as an all-pervading substance is conjoined with another all-pervading substance because it is a substance, like a jar; likewise, an all-pervading substance is conjoined with God because it is a substance, like a jar; and God is conjoined with time and so forth because He is a substance, like a jar—by such arguments, the conjunction of all-pervading substances is established.

Now, regarding *śakti* (power): *Śakti* is a certain non-substantial entity (*adravyaviśeṣa*) that serves as the basis for the causal efficiency of all causes. Its existence is established through both reasoning (*tarka*) and scripture (*āgama*). Indeed, when an obstructing magnet, mantra, or the like is present, fire does not burn even though there is no deficiency in its own nature or its auxiliary factors; that which prevents this is the supersensible (*atīndriya*) power. This is well-known in the case of magnets and similar objects. That power resides in six types of substances. Its residence in the Blessed Lord (*Bhagavat*) is well-known from the *Purāṇaratna* and other texts. Thus, in every case, the existence of a specific property named "power" is established.
Regarding the inclusion of the twenty-four qualities within the ten qualities accepted by the Vaiśeṣikas:

if it is asked, "Since it has been stated that there are twenty-four kinds of qualities, how can they be specified as being only ten?", the answer is as follows: The six qualities of the living self (jīva)—namely, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort—are included within cognition, because they are said to be expansions of cognition. Furthermore, merit (dharma) and demerit (adharma) are included within the cognition of the Lord (Īśvara), because they consist of the Lord's cognition in the form of satisfaction or dissatisfaction. And the mental impression (saṃskāra) known as *bhāvanā* is included because it is a specific form of cognition.

This is because the *saṃskāra* known as velocity (*vega*) is established solely from the cause that produces upward motion; because the *sthitasthāpaka* [elasticity] is also possible by taking conjunction (*saṃyoga*) as its basis; because the five qualities—sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—are accepted as being established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); because even disjunction (*vibhāga*) and separateness (*pṛthaktva*) are established by taking the absence of conjunction as their basis; because priority (*paratva*) and posteriority (*aparatva*) are established by taking specific conjunctions with space and time as their basis; and because number, dimension, fluidity, and viscidity are established by taking the very nature of their respective substances as their basis.
And since it is appropriate to include heaviness within [the category of] power (*śakti*), it is well said that there are exactly ten;
for each of those respective qualities has its own respective substratum (*dharmin*).

In this context, *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are the qualities (*guṇa*) of *prakṛti*, as well as the qualities of the individual soul (*jīva*) associated with it. The notion that "knowledge is of the nature of *sattva*" or "time is *sāttvika*" is merely figurative (*aupacārikī*), arising from the influence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). The five [objects] beginning with sound are well known as the qualities of the five gross elements (*mahābhūta*), which are the effects of *prakṛti*. Pure *sattva* (*śuddhasattva*), however, exists in the manifestation consisting of three-quarters (*tripādvibhūti*) and in the Lord who impels it. The distinction is that the two qualities in the form of the power of conjunction (*saṃyogaśakti*) are common to all six categories of substance (*ṣaḍdravya*). Thus, non-substance (*adravya*) has been defined.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of Non-Substances," in the *Yatīndramatadīpikā*, a treatise on the technical terminology of the Śārīraka [Mīmāṃsā], composed by Śrīnivāsadāsa, the first disciple of the illustrious Mahācārya, the ornament of the Vādhūla lineage.
